text: Howlett says Pico's universe joins the Latin emphasis on positive theology with the negative theology prominent in Byzantine Orthodoxy, at a time of renewed interest in Pseudo-Dionysius.

quotes.text: It brings together the Latin world’s preoccupation with the relationship between reason and faith, and its emphasis on kataphatic (positive) theology, with the negative or apophatic theology so important in Byzantine Orthodoxy, at a time of renewed interest in writers such as Pseudo-Dionysius.

judged.justification: Frames Pico's apophaticism as a conscious Latin-Byzantine synthesis.

text: Howlett holds that in Pico's ladder the positive attributes of God structure the ascent, while what God is not lies beyond the ladder and beyond the universe.

quotes.text: The ladder is built out of what God is—the positive (describable) attributes. Beyond the ladder, beyond our universe, is the realm of what God is not….

text: Howlett describes the mystical tradition of Pseudo-Dionysius as the living spirit that binds together the Platonic, Aristotelian and Kabbalistic parts of Pico's world.

quotes.text: Christianity, particularly the mystical tradition expressed through Pseudo-Dionysius and others, is the living spirit of his world, binding everything together.

text: Howlett notes that Platonism and Christianity are already combined in Pseudo-Dionysius' account of henosis and suggests that Pico was largely unaware of such prior connections.

quotes.text: For example, Platonism and Christianity are already combined in Pseudo-Dionysius’ version of henosis. We should assume that Pico was largely unaware of these connections.

open_questions.text: Howlett assumes rather than shows Pico's unawareness of the Platonism already inside Dionysius.

text: Howlett says that because Ficino's Platonism was still evolving, Pico could assert a Platonism in contradiction to Ficino's and claim a purer reading through Plotinus, and that contradicting Ficino is arguably axiomatic to his work.

quotes.text: This means that Pico could assert his Platonism in contradiction to Ficino’s, challenge Ficino’s authority by emphasizing alternative aspects of Plato and claim a ‘purer’ (rightly or wrongly) reading than Ficino’s in his use of Plotinus, for example. This challenge is so consistent that contradicting Ficino is arguably axiomatic to his work.

bears_on.note: contradicting Ficino as a consistent stance

judged.justification: Makes the quarrel with Ficino a structural feature of Pico's work rather than an episode.

text: Howlett points out that Ficino's Platonism was not pure either, being influenced by his antecedents such as Aquinas and combined with Christianity.

quotes.text: Confusingly, Ficino is not ‘purely’ a Platonist either. He is seeking to combine elements of Plato (and his followers) with Christianity; and inevitably is influenced by his historical milieu and antecedents, such as Aquinas.

bears_on.note: Aquinas as an influence on Ficino

text: Howlett says Pico's Enneads use in 1486 preceded Ficino's published translation, so his Platonism belonged to a revival still in progress.

quotes.text: Pico’s use of Plotinus’ Enneads. In 1486, for example, occurred before Ficino had published a translation. So, when Pico talks about Platonism, he is talking about a revival in progress.

bears_on.note: Pico reached Plotinus ahead of Ficino's translation

text: Howlett argues that Pico challenges Ficino not because he is an Aristotelian but because he believes himself closer to the real Plato, and also to assert his own abilities.

quotes.text: He does not consistently challenge Ficino, for example, because he is an Aristotelian, but because he believes he is closer to the ‘real’ Plato, than Ficino. He also challenges Ficino because of his desire to assert his own abilities.

bears_on.note: motive for Pico's disagreement with Ficino

judged.justification: Denies that the quarrel is simply Aristotle against Plato.

text: Pico reportedly told Ficino his purpose was to compare Plato with Aristotle, and Aristotle with Plato, in alternate studies.

quotes.text: He tells Ficino ‘My purpose was that with the full strength of my mind and my utmost perseverance and diligence, I might now compare Plato with Aristotle, and in turn Aristotle with Plato, in alternate studies.’

bears_on.note: Pico's stated programme in writing to Ficino

text: Howlett reports that Pico's aim moved from alternating study of Plato and Aristotle to showing their compatibility, a desire that persisted until 1490.

quotes.text: But this impulse rapidly moved to the idea of providing a concordance. In his 1484 letter to Barbaro, he explains that while he may have begun working on Plato as an attempt to explore beyond Aristotle, he now had the overwhelming desire to show how the two philosophers are compatible. This desire does not go away. In 1490, we find him working ‘continuously on the Concordia of Plato and Aristotle.’

bears_on.note: 1484 letter states desire for concord

text: Howlett says that Pico learned Platonism in large part from Ficino and had conversations on Kabbalism from an Aristotelian Jew, preferring Kabbalistic commentaries influenced by Maimonides.

quotes.text: He had conversations on Kabbalism from an Aristotelian Jew and learned Platonism in large part from Ficino. He starts as an Averroist Aristotelian with a love of mathematics, and a strong interest in contemporary scholastic debates. He becomes interested in Kabbalism tending to prefer Kabbalistic commentaries that are influenced by the Jewish Averroist Aristotelian, Moses Maimonides.

bears_on.note: Pico learned Platonism in large part from Ficino

text: Howlett says Aquinas in the thirteenth century tried to marry Aristotelianism with Christianity, and that Ficino built his union of faith and reason on Platonism and Christianity following Augustine.

quotes.text: Various solutions were proposed, for instance in the thirteenth century, Aquinas attempted to marry Aristotelianism with Christianity20;
Ficino followed St. Augustine, building his union on a revitalized relationship between Platonism and Christianity.

bears_on.note: Ficino's Augustinian route to reconciling faith and reason contrasted with Pico's

text: Howlett says Pico attempted something more ambitious, maintaining parts of scholasticism as well as Plato and other ancient wisdom in one grand concordance between philosophy and Christianity.

quotes.text: Pico attempted something rather more ambitious, maintaining parts of scholasticism as well as Plato and other forms of ancient wisdom to build a grand concordance between philosophy and Christianity.

bears_on.note: different scope of project from Ficino's

judged.justification: Sets the Ficino/Pico difference at the level of project scope.

text: Howlett says Pico tended toward Aquinas and the via antiqua, whose realism made Aristotle the philosopher, while remaining sympathetic to the Paris conversations of the via moderna.

quotes.text: Aquinas, for instance, a standard-bearer for the realist approach, called Aristotle ‘the philosopher,’ i.e., the ultimate authority. But by Pico’s time, the arguments between realism and nominalism had become increasingly obscure. Pico tended toward Aquinas and the via antiqua, however sympathetic he was to the conversations in Paris, the center for the via moderna.

text: Howlett says Ficino and Pico began as teacher and student in the early 1480s and that their relationship was complex both in life and after Pico's death.

quotes.text: Ficino and Pico began as teacher and student in the early 1480s. But their relationship was complex both in life and after Pico’s death.

bears_on.note: teacher and student in the early 1480s

text: Howlett argues that Ficino encouraged a story of intellectual proximity, casting Pico as heir-apparent of a Platonic Academy and crafting after Pico's death a narrative aligning Pico's birth and arrival in Florence with Ficino's Platonic work.

quotes.text: This story of the Academy had Ficino at the center, as leader of the Platonic revival, with Pico playing ‘heir-apparent,’ as the young philosopher-prince. Pico is the Princeps Concordiae of this Academy49 described by Ficino as a hero or demi-God.50 Ficino encouraged this story of their intellectual proximity for posterity crafting a narrative after Pico’s death which aligned the young hero’s birth with the beginnings of Ficino’s study of Platonism, and Pico’s arrival in Florence with Ficino’s publication of Plato’s works.

bears_on.note: Ficino's posthumous narrative of Pico as heir

judged.justification: Treats the Academy story as Ficino's self-fashioning, so Pico's departures from Ficino need no explaining away.

text: Howlett says the reading of Ficino and Pico as members of one group makes Pico essentially a Platonist and Pico's deviations from Ficino very confusing, while works on Pico alone tend to sideline Ficino almost completely.

quotes.text: This reading of Ficino and Pico portrays Pico as essentially a Platonist52 making Pico’s deviations from Ficino or outright contradic-tions very confusing.
These works tend to sideline Ficino almost completely, to the point where comparisons and influence disappear. It is almost as if Ficino does not exist in Pico’s story.

bears_on.note: two competing historiographies of the relationship

judged.justification: Identifies both received framings as distorting.

text: Howlett says that Ficino's letters show Pico involved in more than a fifth of Ficino's correspondence between 1484 and 1488, and that Ficino responds to Pico's demands with praise, attempting to gloss over their disagreements.

quotes.text: He is involved in more than a fifth of Ficino’s correspondence between 1484 and 1488,54 whether demanding books from Ficino’s library, or annoyed at Ficino’s constant mythologizing of their relationship. The picture from these letters is of Ficino as the benevolent teacher willing to guide and forgive all, and an occasionally tetchy, recalcitrant but brilliant pupil. Pico demands or antagonizes, Ficino responds with more praise, attempting to gloss over their disagreements.

bears_on.note: tone of the letters: Pico antagonizes, Ficino smooths

judged.justification: Gives the letters' pattern of antagonism and smoothing.

text: Howlett holds that the debates between Ficino and Pico are the points of rupture, where they specifically and publicly engage each other.

quotes.text: The debates between Ficino and Pico are the points of rupture—the places where they specifically and publicly engage with each other.

bears_on.note: debates as the public points of rupture

text: Howlett says Pico sent a draft of his Commentary to Ficino and that Lorenzo asked Ficino to invite Pico to live in Florence on his return to Italy, showing a close relationship.

quotes.text: Pico sends a draft of his Commentary to Ficino, and it is Ficino who Lorenzo asks to invite Pico to live in Florence upon his return to Italy.59 It is clearly a close relationship.

bears_on.note: draft of the Commentary sent to Ficino; Ficino as inviter
Lorenzo asks Ficino to invite Pico

text: Howlett notes that Ficino's collected letters include no letters about, and no mention of, Pico's De ente.

quotes.text: Ficino also does not include any letters in his collected letters or mention of Pico’s On Being and the One.

bears_on.note: silence on De ente in Ficino's collected letters

judged.justification: Notes the absence of the dispute from Ficino's published correspondence.

text: Howlett says a curious silence falls in the correspondence in 1493-94 and that the relationship was complicated by Pico's constant written disagreement with Ficino and perhaps more by the ascendance of Savonarola.

quotes.text: The only major gap in their epistolary relationship is between 1493 and 94, when a curious silence falls.60 The relationship was no doubt complicated by Pico’s constant written disagreement with Ficino’s positions, but perhaps more importantly this is the period of Savonarola’s ascendance.

bears_on.note: 1493-94 gap in the letters
Savonarola's ascendance as context for the silence

text: Howlett writes that up until 1493 it is as if Pico and Ficino are in a decade-long argument, expressed as a series of debates on the position of Beauty and finally on the influence of the stars, though Ficino remained always close to Pico.

quotes.text: Up until 1493 it is as if Ficino and Pico are in a decade-long argument, expressed as a series of debates or ruptures whether on the position of Beauty in the universe or, right at the end, the influence of the stars on our lives. But Ficino was always close to Pico

bears_on.note: decade-long argument in debates

text: Howlett says Pico's request to Benivieni to change his poem let him give a reading of Plotinus truer to the original than Ficino's Platonism of the time, and that Ficino claimed after Pico's death that Pico renounced the work.

quotes.text: Pico’s request to Benivieni to change his poem allowed him to make a more ‘true to the original’ reading of Plotinus than Ficino’s brand of Platonism at the time, asserting both the primacy of Plotinus and his own reading of Enneads. Pico’s comments were later smoothed over and Ficino claimed after his death that Pico ‘renounced’ this work.

bears_on.note: first disagreement with Ficino; Ficino's later 'renounced' claim

text: Howlett characterises the Commentary episode as essentially a cover-up permitted in large part because Pico did not publish the Commentary or live long enough to complete a self-fashioning of his career.

quotes.text: In the case of Ficino, there is essentially a ‘cover-up’ permitted in large part because Pico did not publish the Commentary and did not live long enough even to complete a self-fashioning of his career.

bears_on.note: the cover-up of the Ficino disagreement

text: Howlett summarises De ente as arguing that God is both singular (the One) and Being, and that Plato and Aristotle agree on this.

quotes.text: In 1491, Pico circulated On Being and the One. This is a short piece arguing that God ... is both singular (the One) and Being. He argues that Plato and Aristotle agree on this.

bears_on.note: the thesis Ficino contested

text: Howlett reports that Plato is normally understood to posit that the One is above Being, particularly in the Parmenides, differing from Aristotle who places the two together.

quotes.text: Plato is normally understood to posit that the One is above Being, particularly in his dialogue Parmenides; differing from Aristotle who places the two together.

bears_on.note: the received view Pico opposed

text: Howlett says De ente was Pico's last completed manuscript and may have been meant as part of his Concordance of Plato and Aristotle, as he seems to indicate.

quotes.text: On Being and the One was Pico’s last completed manuscript and it may have been meant to be part of his Concordance of Plato and Aristotle (or so he seems to indicate).

hedge_words: it may have been meant to be part of his Concordance of Plato and Aristotle (or so he seems to indicate)

text: Howlett argues that to reach concord in De ente Pico had to remove obstacles in Plato, particularly the Parmenides, which he treats as merely a rhetorical exercise, so that Plato should not be taken at his word.

quotes.text: To achieve concord in this case, he needed to remove several obstacles in Plato, particularly Parmenides. Pico argues that the dialogue is simply a rhetorical exercise, meaning that we should not take Plato at his word.

bears_on.note: Pico's treatment of the Parmenides is the point contested by Ficino

judged.justification: Presents the rhetorical-exercise reading as a means to concord.

text: Howlett says Ficino translated the Parmenides around 1469 but had probably not yet written a commentary when Pico wrote De ente, and that his commentary was published in 1496.

quotes.text: In 1496, a few years after Pico’s death, Ficino published his Commentary on Plato’s ‘Parmenides’. Ficino had translated Parmenides around 1469 but had probably not yet written a commentary when Pico wrote On Being and the One.

open_questions.text: Whether Ficino's commentary was written before or after De ente is stated with a hedge.

bears_on.note: chronology of the Parmenides commentary

text: Howlett argues that a commentary produced between 1492 and 1494, while Pico was still living, follows a sequence that takes on Pico's arguments section by section to refute him.

quotes.text: Between 1492 and 1494, while Pico was still living, he produced the commentary. It follows a sequence that specifically takes on Pico’s arguments section by section to refute him.

warrants.text: Howlett's note cites Van Haelen (2009) for this point.

bears_on.note: Ficino's Parmenides commentary as a section-by-section reply to De ente

judged.justification: Makes the Parmenides commentary a direct refutation of De ente rather than an independent work.

text: Howlett says Ficino held to the Platonic orthodoxy, deriving from Plotinus and often filtered through Proclus, that Plato argues the One is above Being.

quotes.text: Ficino himself holds with Platonic orthodoxy, deriving from Plotinus, often filtered through Proclus, that Plato argues the One is above Being.

bears_on.note: Ficino's orthodox position on the One

text: Howlett argues that De ente was already partly an attack on Ficino, who had written on Being and the One even before his commentary and consistently held the orthodox Platonic view placing the two separately.

quotes.text: Ficino is providing a contemporaneous direct reply and counter to Pico. But On Being was already partly an attack on Ficino. Even before his commentary, Ficino had written about Being and the One and was consistently of the ‘orthodox’ Platonic view placing the two separately.

bears_on.note: De ente as an attack on Ficino's published view

judged.justification: Reverses the assumed order: Ficino's commentary answers a work already aimed at Ficino.

text: Howlett notes that this controversy has often been discussed and that Salas has taken apart some inconsistencies in Pico's argumentation.

quotes.text: This particular conflict has been discussed often, for instance by Van Haelen (2009), Allen (1995, for example), and Salas (2014) who has taken apart some of the inconsistencies in Pico’s argumentation.

bears_on.note: secondary literature on the Parmenides-De ente controversy

text: Howlett summarises the three major polemical moments as Ficino's Symposium commentary answered by Pico's Commentary, Ficino's traditional view of God as the One above Being answered by De ente, and Ficino's Parmenides commentary in reply.

quotes.text: Ficino writes his Commentary on Plato’s ‘Symposium,’ Pico counters with his Commentary. More loosely in time, Ficino clearly adopts and champions a traditional Platonic view of God as the One above Being. Pico responds with On Being and the One. Ficino counters with his Commentary on Plato’s ‘Parmenides.’

bears_on.note: three exchanges in sequence

judged.justification: Gives a compact sequence for the dispute.

text: Howlett says Ficino wished to correct Pico or smooth over the cracks, and that the pattern of confrontation indicates a larger disagreement of purpose or mission between two philosophers whose sources are not so different.

quotes.text: Pico wishes to take on Ficino. Ficino wishes to ‘correct’ Pico or smooth over the cracks. This is not simply an acrimonious personal relationship, a chance for the former student to ‘one-up’ his teacher, or two philosophers in the same town with very different views who are bound to disagree. This is part of an overall pattern of confrontation indicating a larger and more important disagreement—a disagreement of purpose between two philosophers whose sources and inclinations are not so very different, but whose purposes are.

bears_on.note: disagreement of purpose rather than of sources

judged.justification: Relocates the quarrel from doctrine to mission.

text: Howlett says the question of mission has become clearer for Ficino in the past twenty years of scholarship through the concept of renovatio, using a Platonized Christianity to aim at a new Golden World through the return to God, but that such a mission has not been so defined in Pico's case.

quotes.text: Rather there is the question of mission. This question of mission has become clearer in the case of Ficino in the past 20 years of scholarship through the concept of renovatio: using a Platonized Christianity he aims at the formation of a new Golden World through the return to God (marrying reason once again with faith). But in Pico’s case, such a mission has not been so defined.

bears_on.note: Ficino's renovatio mission

text: Howlett argues both Ficino and Pico use Aristotle, Ficino drawing on Aquinas and the peripatetics for analogia entis, act and potency and his theory of Being, so that there is an effort at concord between Aristotle and Plato in Ficino too.

quotes.text: First, both Ficino and Pico use Aristotle. ... He also never denies the importance of Aristotle, using both the philosopher and his later commentators, especially Aquinas, in his work, for instance the Aristotelian-Thomistic tradition of analogia entis, the Aristotelian example of act and potency, and most importantly often using the peripatetics in his theory of Being. There is an effort at concord here between Aristotle and Plato

bears_on.note: Aquinas and Aristotle in Ficino's theory of Being

judged.justification: Places Aquinas and peripatetic doctrine inside Ficino's own theory of Being.

text: Howlett says Ficino and Pico both use Proclus, Pico using him in 100 of the 900 conclusions, and that Ficino draws on Proclus' Platonic Theology when discussing God as Unity.

quotes.text: Pico uses Proclus more times than any other thinker in his Conclusions (100 out of 900 conclusions),85 and disputed with Ficino in his Commentary on Plotinian grounds. Ficino also uses Proclus’ Platonic Theology when discussing the attributes of God (God as Unity [book 1.20], Truth [1.21] and Beauty [1.24]) in his own Platonic Theology.86

bears_on.note: shared reliance on Proclus

text: Howlett states in a note that Ficino emphasizes one God rather than the Proclan universe of henads, whereas Pico's Kabbalism lets him explore Proclus in all his complexity.

quotes.text: Where they deviate is Ficino emphasizes one God rather than the Proclan baroque universe of henads, see Dillon (2011, 14–15), whereas Pico’s Kabbalism allows him to explore Proclus in all this complexity.

warrants.text: Note cites Dillon (2011) for the point on henads.

bears_on.note: where Ficino's use of Proclus differs from Pico's

judged.justification: Names the point where the Proclus borrowings diverge.

text: Howlett argues Pico is remarkable in going back to Plotinus, the point of origin of Neoplatonism, emphasizing him more than Ficino did at the time.

quotes.text: Pico is remarkable for his moment in that he went back to Plotinus, the point of origin for Neoplatonism emphasizing him at the time more than Ficino.

bears_on.note: Plotinus weighted differently

text: Howlett says Plotinus' emphasis on the One, easily equated with God, allowed Neoplatonism to develop into an increasingly elaborate theological philosophy, and that it is unsurprising that Proclus' key work was the Platonic Theology, from which Ficino took the title of his own summa.

quotes.text: Plotinus’ emphasis on the One, easily equitable with God, allowed Neoplatonism to develop into such a structure. Platonism became that most sacred of philosophies. It is unsurprising then that Proclus’ summa or key work was the Platonic Theology, from which Ficino took the title for his own summa.

bears_on.note: Ficino's summa titled after Proclus

text: Howlett argues that Pico's use of Plato and Aristotle in De ente is awkward because he attempts a change in the Platonic universe in an effort, he claims, to return to an original understanding of Plato, sidelining the Parmenides as a rhetorical exercise.

quotes.text: The use of Plato and Aristotle in On Being and the One is awkward because he is attempting a change in the Platonic universe, but he does so in an effort, he claims, to return to an original understanding of Plato (perhaps thinking of the skepticism of the Middle Academy period). This claim includes his sidelining of Plato’s Parmenides as a rhetorical exercise: a surprising and odd argument.

hedge_words: perhaps thinking of the skepticism of the Middle Academy period

text: Howlett says Pico asserts he is more militantly originalist than Ficino: in the Commentary he criticises Ficino for using intermediaries on Plotinus, and in De ente he says he is going back to the real Plato rather than seeing him through Proclus.

quotes.text: Pico asserts he is even more militantly originalist than Ficino: part of his critique in the Commentary is that Ficino is utilizing intermediaries to discuss Plotinus and fails to go back to the source. In On Being and the One he argues he is going back to the real Plato rather than seeing him through the faulty lens of Proclus, for instance (despite his copious use of Proclus).89

bears_on.note: originalism as the ground of Pico's challenge

judged.justification: Shows De ente's anti-Proclus posture as part of the quarrel with Ficino's Neoplatonism.

text: Howlett states in a note that Farmer suggests Ficino's use of Proclus came after Pico's Conclusions.

quotes.text: Indeed, Farmer suggests that Ficino’s use of Proclus came after Pico’s Conclusions (1998, 20).

bears_on.note: priority in using Proclus

text: Howlett argues Ficino tied the ancient theologians together through Platonism into a Platonic-Christian hybrid, while Pico tied them within a Platonic structure using Aristotelian argument and Kabbalism.

quotes.text: But Ficino tied these strands together through Platonism and creates a Platonic–Christian hybrid. Pico attempts to tie them all together within a Platonic understanding of the structure of the universe while ... using Aristotelian argumentation and Kabbalism, which he understands to be part of the prisca theologia.

bears_on.note: two ways of tying the prisca theologia together

text: Howlett quotes Kristeller that there can be no doubt as to Pico's dependence on Ficino, and says much of Pico's work would not have been possible without Ficino's translations and commentaries.

quotes.text: But as Kristeller argues, ‘There can be no doubt… as to Pico’s dependence on Ficino.’91 Whether in his Commentary, Oration, or Heptaplus, we see evidence of the Platonic revival, and just as with other aspects of Pico’s legacy, much of what Pico produced would not have been possible without Ficino’s translations and commentaries

bears_on.note: Pico's dependence on Ficino

text: Howlett says both Ficino and Pico agreed on connecting metaphysics with theology, bringing faith and reason together, which distinguishes them from the scholastics.

quotes.text: Both agreed—and this is a crucial part of their work—on the need to connect their metaphysics with theology, bringing faith and reason back together. This is a clear distinction between Ficino, Pico, and the scholastics, for example.

bears_on.note: shared aim

text: Howlett notes that Pico's Disputations indirectly attacks Ficino's astrological magic in the third book of De vita, and that this dispute is unconnected to questions of Platonism against Aristotelianism.

quotes.text: Disputations, Pico’s unfinished polemic against astrology, indirectly attacks Ficino’s comments on astrological magic in his third book of De vita libri tres, De vita coelitus comparanda (1489).
Pico was entering a conversation about astrology that had been going for centuries,65 unconnected to questions of Platonism against Aristotelianism or variations of the same.

bears_on.note: astrology dispute distinct from the One dispute

text: Howlett says it is unclear whether Pico is inconsistent on astrology, making a point about science or political prediction, or whether Disputations is a patchwork of Pico and Gianfrancesco's editing.

quotes.text: It is unclear whether he is inconsistent in his views, is making a particular point around his preconceived view of ‘science,’ has a specific message concerning political predictions (and other areas of astrology become partially ‘involved’ perhaps to contradict further Ficino) or whether Disputations is a patchwork of Pico and Gianfrancesco’s editing.79

open_questions.text: Whether the Disputations attack on astrology is consistent, or edited by Gianfrancesco.

basis_quote.text: It is unclear whether he is inconsistent in his views

bears_on.note: astrology dispute uncertain in motive

text: Howlett notes there are other, less well explored conflicts between Pico and Ficino such as Pico's discussion of human nature in the Heptaplus and Oration.

quotes.text: There are other ongoing conflicts between Pico and Ficino, though less well explored, such as Pico’s discussion of human nature in his Heptaplus and Oration.80

bears_on.note: other conflicts on human nature

text: Howlett says that without the Academy framework Pico is no longer Ficino's closest protege and that the Academy perspective required arguing that Pico was mistaken in De ente and Ficino gently correcting him.

quotes.text: Without the Academy perspective, Pico is no longer Ficino’s closest protege, bound to him as an acolyte and we can no longer assume the same goals. Within the Academy perspective, we needed to argue that Pico did not really mean to undermine Ficino’s work on astrology, but was attacking prophets, for instance, who used the stars; or that Pico was mistaken ... in his argumentation in On Being and the One, and Ficino was gently correcting him.

bears_on.note: Academy framework distorts the reading of De ente

judged.justification: Removes the harmonising reading of the De ente exchange.

text: Howlett notes that concord first appears as a linguistic matter and quotes Pico's thesis that Aristotle and Plato agree in meaning and substance in every natural or divine question, though in their words they seem to disagree.

quotes.text: As Pico says ‘There is no natural or divine question in which Aristotle and Plato do not agree in meaning and substance, although in their words they seem to disagree.’119

text: Howlett cites Pico as finding, on examining the two, that in the words nothing is more opposed and in the substance nothing is more concordant.

quotes.text: For in examining the two, he finds that ‘if you examine the words (verba), nothing is more opposed; if you examine the substance (res), nothing is more concordant.’

text: Howlett says Pico's Aristotelianism supplies his mode of argument, including insistence on dividing causal from participatory being, while his universe is predominantly a Platonic one inflected by Aristotle.

quotes.text: Aristotelianism provides his mode of argumentation (insistence on dividing causal from participatory being, for example)
At the macro level, Pico’s deep structure is predominantly a Platonic universe inflected by Aristotle.

open_questions.text: How the causal/participatory distinction operates in De ente is not developed at this point.

text: Howlett says Pico's aim is to show that philosophy leads to theology and then to religious faith, echoing Pseudo-Dionysius.

quotes.text: We need philosophy, which takes us to theology and then to religious faith, to echo Pseudo-Dionysius.112

warrants.text: Howlett's note cites Trinkaus (1987) for the Dionysian echo.

text: Howlett argues Pico's concordance hierarchizes the process, so resolution can lean toward one side, which perhaps explains why his Aristotelianism and Platonism seem to alternate.

quotes.text: Indeed, Pico’s structure consistently hierarchizes the process of concordance: resolution can lean toward one argument over another.114 This is perhaps why the conversation between Pico’s Aristotelianism and Platonism is so complicated: sometimes he appears to favor Aristotelianism, and at other times gives a more Platonic answer.

warrants.text: Note cites De Boer (2009) for the hierarchical character of Pico's syncretism.

text: Howlett says Pico and Ficino both believed that the earlier the knowledge, the truer it is likely to be.

quotes.text: Pico, and Ficino, believed that the earlier the knowledge, the more primary or ‘truer’ it is likely to be

bears_on.note: shared assumption about priority of origin

text: Howlett states that Cardinal Bessarion espoused concordism between Aristotle and Plato.

quotes.text: ‘Concordism’ as a term is particularly associated with forming agreement between Aristotle and Plato. It was espoused by Cardinal Bessarion, one of the earliest proponents of the new Greek Studies.110

text: Howlett quotes a note that Pico did not hold that all philosophers defended the same position in different words, and that he privileged the claims of Christianity.

quotes.text: Pico ‘did not espouse the view that all philosophers were defending the same position using different terms and expressions; Pico privileges the claims of Christianity and sought external confirmations of them.’

open_questions.text: Pico's concord may not be identity of doctrine; the note qualifies the main text's reading.

text: Howlett reports Schmitt's view that Aquinas was primarily Aristotelian in form but Platonic in his metaphysics, though distinguishing the two was difficult at the time.

quotes.text: Schmitt (1983, 29) and also argues that Aquinas was primarily in form Aristotelian, but in his metaphysics, Platonic, though distinguishing was difficult at the time (1983, 93).

judged.justification: Aquinas as already Platonic in metaphysics complicates any Aristotle/Plato divide.

text: Howlett reports from Garin that Del Medigo was with Pico in Perugia, where they spent much time talking about being, essence and unity.

quotes.text: Garin (2008, 303) states Medigo was with him in Perugia where they spent a lot of time ‘talking about being, essence, and unity.’

warrants.text: Note cites Garin (2008) and Mahoney (1972) for the conversations.

open_questions.text: The note does not date the Perugia conversations in the quotation.

text: Howlett says Ficino uses the prisca theologia to lead a renovatio, whereas Pico seeks the esoteric primarily for private revelation, and that Kabbalism did not have such a distinctive role in Ficino.

quotes.text: Ficino uses the prisca theologia to access hidden or lost secrets that can be used to lead a renovatio: the transformation of our world into a new Platonic Christian Golden Age. Pico seeks the esoteric, individualistic, contemplative, and exclusive primarily, at least by the time of his death, for private revelation.
Finally, he emphasizes Kabbalism as part of the line (Kabbalism did not have such a distinctive role in Ficino).

bears_on.note: difference in use of the prisca theologia

text: Howlett reports Hankins's series of essays contesting the twentieth-century norm of a Platonic Academy in Florence led by Ficino and including Pico.

quotes.text: The question of the existence of a Platonic Academy in Florence led by Marsilio Ficino and including Pico, historically suggested by Armando della Torre, Storia dell’Accademia Platonica di Firenze (History of the Platonic Academy of Florence, Florence, 1902) and established as a scholarly norm during the twentieth century, was contested in a series of essays by James Hankins.

bears_on.note: the Academy framework contested

text: Howlett reports in a note that in reply to Ficino's invitation to live in Florence Pico addressed Ficino as father of the Platonic family and master of his learning.

quotes.text: Replying to Ficino’s invitation to live in Florence, Pico addresses Ficino as ‘father of the Platonic family,’ his life’s ‘solace,’ his mind’s ‘delight,’ conduct’s ‘guide’ and learning’s ‘master’ (disciplinae magister).

warrants.text: Note attributes the report to Allen (2008) citing Ficino's Opera.

bears_on.note: Pico's deferential address to Ficino

text: Howlett reports Farmer's argument that Pico's new philosophy lay in a traditional though exaggerated Neoplatonic framework tied to the highly syncretic Platonic systems of late antiquity.

quotes.text: Farmer (1998, 19) argues that ‘Pico’s “new philosophy” lay in a traditional, though exaggerated, Neo-Platonic framework, with special ties to those high-syncretic Platonic systems developed in antiquity after Plotinus….’

text: Howlett says the Conclusions show Pico's three pillars: in section one the largest cohort is medieval philosophy led by Aquinas, then Platonists led by Proclus, and the largest individual sections belong to Proclus, then Kabbalism, then Aquinas, then Averroes.

quotes.text: Of all the conclusions in section one the majority are from medieval western philosophy, with a large Aristotelianism cohort, led by Aquinas. The second largest number are from Platonists led by Proclus, and the third from ancients led by Kabbalism. The largest number of individual sections belong to Proclus, then Kabbalism, then Aquinas, then Averroes.

text: Howlett says that in Plotinian terms the Kabbalistic Tree can be taken as the many and the God beyond it, the Ein-Sof, as the One, a hidden, unknowable God of whom one can say only what it is not, as in Christian apophatic theology such as Pseudo-Dionysius.

quotes.text: We could argue in Plotinian terms that the Tree is the many, and the unity beyond the Tree, the One. This God beyond is hidden, unknowable, infinite, and formless. In Hebrew it is called the Ein-Sof.13 We cannot say what it is, we can only say what it is not, much as we would in Christian negative (apophatic) theology (such as in Pseudo-Dionysius), as opposed to the kataphatic theology of the Catholic church.

judged.justification: Sets Kabbalistic Ein-Sof beside the Plotinian One and Dionysian apophasis.

text: Howlett says the Ein-Sof is also called Being, possibly through Aristotelian influences, though indeterminate being, and that in the philosophical setting of Aristotelians versus Platonists it becomes part of the argument around Being and the One.

quotes.text: It is also Being (potentially through Aristotelian influences), but indeterminate being as opposed to the active being we might see within creation.15 Entering the philosophical environment of Aristotelians vs Platonists, the Ein-Sof becomes part of the argument around Being and the One.

warrants.text: Note cites Scholem (1987) for Ein-Sof as Being.

open_questions.text: Whether the Ein-Sof is above being (nought) or indeterminate being is left open in the discussion that follows.

basis_quote.text: If the Ein-Sof is indeterminate being, for example, we could argue that this nought is not God either

judged.justification: Ties Kabbalistic Ein-Sof to the same Being/One issue as De ente.

text: Howlett reports that Isaac's circle emphasized the hidden God with the new term Ein-Sof, beyond the Tree of Life and above divine thought, as cause of Thought beyond being or thought.

quotes.text: For instance, Isaac emphasized the hidden God with the new term Ein-Sof beyond the Tree of Life, as beyond contemplation and above the divine thought expressed in the Tree. This is ‘the cause of Thought,’75 beyond being or thought.

warrants.text: Note cites Scholem (1987, 265) for 'the cause of Thought'.

text: Howlett argues Pico embraces the Ein-Sof as the unity beyond the sefirot, thereby combining Kabbalah with the Plotinian One through a Platonic version of Kabbalism espoused by the Girona School.

quotes.text: For instance, Pico embraces the Ein-Sof concept as the unity beyond the sefirot,196 thereby combining Kabbalah and the Plotinian One using a Platonic version of Kabbalism espoused by the Girona School.197

warrants.text: Note 196 quotes Pico's Conclusion that the Ein-Sof should not be counted with the other numerations.

quote.text: the Ein-Sof should not be counted with the other numerations, because it is the abstract and uncommunicated unity of those numerations, not the coordinated unity.

judged.justification: Shows Pico himself identifying a Plotinian One beyond the sefirot, before De ente.

text: Howlett says Pico calls the Ein-Sof one, in a passage describing God as infinite, as one and as existing through himself, closed in himself and concealed in the abyss of his darkness.

quotes.text: In the Conclusions (according to his own opinion) he describes the Ein-Sof as one: ‘If God is known in himself as infinite, as one, and as existing through himself, we recognize that nothing proceeds from him, but know his separation from things, and his total closure of himself in himself, and his extreme, profound, and solitary retraction in the remotest recess of his divinity

text: Howlett argues that Keter, given the number one, represents the Ein-Sof within the created universe, so that the Plotinian One raises the question of two Ones, one outside creation and one within.

quotes.text: Keter represents the Ein-Sof within the created universe. It is unity and it is one mathematically. Inevitably, this begs the question where the Plotinian One fits. Are there two Ones? (One outside of creation and One within).

open_questions.text: Whether there are two Ones (outside creation and within) or a nought above the One and many.

basis_quote.text: Are there two Ones? (One outside of creation and One within). Is unity as nought above the One and the many?

judged.justification: Poses the two-Ones puzzle that bears on De ente.

text: Howlett reports a passage of Pico comparing Aristotle's concealing of the more divine philosophy with the way Rabbi Moses the Egyptian's Guide for the Perplexed enfolds the mysteries of the Cabala.

quotes.text: Just as Aristotle disguised and concealed the more divine philosophy, which the ancient philosophers veiled under tales and fables, under the mask of philosophical speculation and in the brevity of words, so Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, in the book the Latins call the Guide for the Perplexed, while in the superficial shell of words appears to move with the philosophers, in hidden insights of a profound sense enfolds the mysteries of the Cabala.

text: Howlett argues the Aristotelian First Cause can be argued as Keter, and the first three sefirot together as the First Cause, each triad mirroring an Aristotelian triad of intellection.

quotes.text: The Aristotelian First Cause can also be argued as Keter: explaining perhaps how there can be such a thing as an ‘unmoved mover’ for certainly the Ein-Sof does not act and does not move. Taken together, the first three sefirot can also comprise the Aristotelian First Cause,220

text: Howlett says the connection between Hokmah and the Active Intellect, made by Maimonides and taken up by Abulafia, is present.

quotes.text: The connection between Hokmah and the Active Intellect made from Maimonides and taken up by Abulafia is present.

text: Howlett says Maimonides argued that the ultimate aim of ascent was the Active Intellect, expressed as Hokmah but also as Enoch, Metatron and the Cherubic realm, the higher Active Intellect.

quotes.text: Maimonides argued that prophecy itself was due to the Active Intellect’s influence on us,89 and that our ultimate aim in ascending to the divine was the Active Intellect itself, expressed as Hokmah, but also as Enoch, Metatron, and the ... Cherubic realm (in other words, the ‘higher’ Active Intellect).90

warrants.text: Notes 89-90 cite Copenhaver (2019).

judged.justification: Links Enoch/Metatron/Cherubim to the Active Intellect through Maimonides.

text: Howlett says Pico links the Metatron with aspects of Orpheus' Pallas, Zoroaster's paternal mind, Hermes' son of God, Pythagoras' wisdom and Parmenides' intelligible sphere.

quotes.text: The Metatron is amalgamated with aspects of Orpheus’ Pallas, Zoroaster’s paternal mind, Hermes Trismegistus’ son of God, Pythagoras’ wisdom, and Parmenides’ intelligible sphere.230

text: Howlett says that in Pico's Kabbalistic scheme the guardians of Orphism are powers in Pseudo-Dionysius and the sefira Din in Kabbalah.

quotes.text: The ‘guardians’ found in Orphism are ‘powers’ in Pseudo-Dionysius, and the sefira, Din, in Kabbalah.

text: Howlett states that Pseudo-Dionysius is probably the closest Christian forebear to Pico's mysticism.

quotes.text: The highly influential, Dionysius the Areopagite (Pseudo-Dionysius) is probably the closest Christian forebear to Pico’s mysticism

text: Howlett says the author of the corpus areopagaticum wrote in the fifth and early sixth century, became influential in Latin Europe in the twelfth century and influenced Aquinas and Eckhart, and became even more popular through Traversari's 1436 translation.

quotes.text: Pseudo-Dionyisus was writing in the fifth and early sixth century with a body of works (corpus areopagaticum) attributed to him, such as the Divine Names, Mystical Theology, and Celestial Hierarchy. In Latin Europe, he became influential in the twelfth century and influenced Aquinas as well as medieval mystics such as Meister Eckhart. In the fourteenth century he became even more popular though Ambrogio Traversari’s 1436 translation.

open_questions.text: The passage says 'the fourteenth century' but dates the Traversari translation to 1436, a fifteenth-century year.

basis_quote.text: In the fourteenth century he became even more popular though Ambrogio Traversari’s 1436 translation.

judged.justification: Gives the Latin transmission of Dionysius through Aquinas to Traversari; the century slip is a flag.

text: Howlett says Pico used Dionysius in the Heptaplus in his description of angelic and celestial worlds and throughout the Oration.

quotes.text: Pico used him in Heptaplus in his description of angelic and celestial worlds, for instance, and throughout the Oration.172
Watts (1987, 290): Pico used him ‘heavily, though not exclusively.’
The highly influential, Dionysius the Areopagite (Pseudo-Dionysius) is probably the closest Christian forebear to Pico’s mysticism

warrants.text: Note 172 cites Watts for Pico's use of Dionysius.

quote.text: Watts (1987, 290): Pico used him ‘heavily, though not exclusively.’

text: Howlett states that Pseudo-Dionysius thought of henosis, the final stage, as seeing God (epopteia), and that in the ascent she describes we have moved beyond the Aristotelian Active Intellect, beyond Being itself, to Platonic henosis.

quotes.text: Pseudo-Dionysius thought of henosis, the final stage, as ‘seeing’ God: so, the highest point is actually epopteia, or gazing, contemplating, perceiving, or learning
We have moved beyond the Aristotelian Active Intellect, beyond Being itself, to Platonic henosis.

text: Howlett says that in combining Pseudo-Dionysius, Platonism, Aristotelianism and Jewish thought it is unclear what henosis would be in Kabbalism and what the roles of Keter and the Ein-Sof are.

quotes.text: But in combining Pseudo-Dionysius, with Platonism, Aristotelianism, and Jewish thought (as Pico is attempting to do), it is unclear what henosis would be in Kabbalism and what is the role of Keter or the Ein-Sof.

open_questions.text: What henosis is in Kabbalism and the role of Keter and the Ein-Sof.

basis_quote.text: it is unclear what henosis would be in Kabbalism and what is the role of Keter or the Ein-Sof

text: Howlett states that Pico changes Pseudo-Dionysius' hierarchy of angels from nine to ten, the number of the sefirot.

quotes.text: Elsewhere, where Pseudo-Dionysius and Kabbalism do not coincide, Pico tries hard to relate Pseudo-Dionysius to Kabbalism. For instance, Pico changes Pseudo-Dionysius’ hierarchy of angels from nine to ten, the number of the sefirot.174

warrants.text: Note 174 cites only Pico's Conclusions 28>2 for the change.

open_questions.text: Whether Conclusion 28>2 shows Pico altering the Dionysian nine to ten, or keeping Dionysian and Hebrew orders distinct; other packets address this.

judged.justification: A strong statement that other scholars in this corpus may dispute.

text: Howlett notes that in the Kabbalistic tree of attributes those attributes nearest the point of origin are most like the divine, which in Platonism is the world of Ideas and in Ficino's Christian Platonism the Angelic Mind.

quotes.text: Just as in Platonism, those attributes closer to the point of origin (in Platonism the world of Ideas, in Ficino’s Christian Platonism, ‘the Angelic Mind’) are most like the divine itself.

bears_on.note: Ficino's Angelic Mind as the Christian Platonic counterpart of the Ideas

text: Howlett says Enoch is synonymous with the Metatron, a high angelic power, and that by the middle of the thirteenth century the Metatron had been divided into a higher, Great Metatron and a lower.

quotes.text: Enoch is also synonymous with the Metatron, a high angelic power or the voice of God. By the middle of the thirteenth century, the Metatron had been divided into a higher or Great Metatron and a lower. Enoch’s role is connected to the active divinity, within creation, and its voice on the Tree of Life, whereas the Great Metatron is now a mystery above and beyond.41

warrants.text: Note 41 supports the Metatron division.

text: Howlett describes Proclus' scheme as triads of henads related to the worlds of the Platonic universe, with orders of angels, demons, heroes and souls below the gods, the triads repeating within an ever more crowded universe.

quotes.text: Proclus used triads of henads, deanthropomorphized gods similar to the gnostic concept of aeons, and related them to the various worlds of the Platonic universe: so the first triad is made up of the intelligible trinity, intelligible-intellectual trinity and intellectual hebdomad

Below are orders of angels, demons, heroes, and souls. But this is not all, the triads repeat themselves within an ... increasingly complex and crowded universe of the divine and semi-divine, all based on the rule of three.

text: Howlett states that Pico drew connections between the Plotinian One as God and the sefirot, the Trinity, angels and demons in a Platonic-gnostic structure, finding in Kabbalism the Platonic universe of Proclus he already knew.

quotes.text: Plotinus posits the One, which for a Christian or a Jew is God; while sefirot, the Trinity, angels, and demons are all easily present in a Platonic/gnostic structure. Pico drew these connections54; while Proclus’ triadic repetitiveness is echoed both in medieval Kabbalism and throughout Pico’s work. In Kabbalism, Pico was able to find the Platonic universe (particularly of Proclus) that he already knew,55

judged.justification: Presents the sefirot as read by Pico through the Plotinian One and Proclus.

text: Howlett says Maimonides' Jewish Aristotelianism eventually impacted Kabbalism but only later, and that the school in question left only a small place for Maimonides.

quotes.text: Maimonides’ Jewish Aristotelianism did eventually impact Kabbalism, but only later.
he and his school were mystics with only a small place for such as Maimonides83

text: Howlett says Recanati could have been the most significant source of Pico's Kabbalistic statements in section one of the Conclusions, with about 25 of 47 and possibly a further 12 deriving from his work, while section two draws more on Abulafia.

quotes.text: He could have been the most significant source for Pico’s Kabbalistic statements in section one of Conclusions, with about 25 of 47 and a possible further 12 deriving from his work.160 Section two has a different set of sources with Abulafia more dominant, aspects of Recanati, notes of Maimonides and the Sefer Yesirah.161

open_questions.text: Extent of influence of sources not read through Flavius's translations is unclear to date.

basis_quote.text: The extent of the influence of other scholars or texts not read through Flavius’ translation is unclear to date

text: Howlett says Pico's sources strongly suggest that the ecstatic theurgical Kabbalism of Abulafia is primary, with Recanati also important.

quotes.text: In summary, Pico’s sources strongly suggest that the ‘ecstatic’ theurgical Kabbalism of Abulafia is primary,169 with Recanati also an important influence.

text: Howlett says Flavius did not translate the Zohar or Sefer Yesirah, but Pico knew of them through commentaries, and Pico was reading missing works such as the Zohar through commentaries with a preferred perspective.

quotes.text: Inevitably Pico was reading missing works, such as the Zohar, through the lens of commentaries that would have a preferred perspective.152
Flavius did not translate the Zohar or Sefer Yesirah, but Pico knew of them through commentaries at the very least

text: Howlett says Ficino references the Bahir through Paul of Burgos while Pico is the first to use the text directly, and that Ficino also knew other Kabbalistic material such as Samuel Sarsa's Sefer meqor hayyim.

quotes.text: Ficino references the work in his On the Christian Religion but through Paul of Burgos. Pico is the first to use the text directly165 (Ficino does know and use Kabbalah beyond Bahir. For instance, Samu’el Sarsa’s Sefer meqor hayyim from the Spanish tradition.166

bears_on.note: Ficino's own Kabbalistic entry points differ from Pico's

judged.justification: Corrects the assumption that Ficino had no Kabbalah.

text: Howlett says Alemanno, a product of the Paduan Aristotelian circle who gravitated toward Maimonides, worked with Pico, though whether before or after the Rome venture is unclear.

quotes.text: Johanan Alemanno worked with Pico while in Florence, but whether before Pico’s Rome adventure or simply after is unclear.139 He was another product of the Paduan Aristotelian circle, and from the same region as Pico. Like Elijah Del Medigo, he had combined his love of Aristotelianism with Judaic and Hebraic studies, naturally gravitating toward Moses Maimonides, as the quintessential Aristotelian Jewish philosopher.140

open_questions.text: Date of the Pico-Alemanno collaboration.

basis_quote.text: whether before Pico’s Rome adventure or simply after is unclear

text: Howlett says Pico's universe is primarily Christian Platonic with attempted concordance with Aristotelianism and Kabbalism, so that Pico's difference from Ficino shows his own contribution, resting in part on a strong preference for Proclus.

quotes.text: The structure of Pico’s universe is primarily Christian Platonic but with attempted concordance at critical points with Aristotelianism and Kabbalism. Ficino’s universe therefore provides a useful starting point from which to begin an analysis. Differences from Ficino are where we can see Pico’s unique contribution which in part relies on his strong preference for Proclus within Platonism, but primarily derives from his project of concordance.

bears_on.note: Pico's structure measured against Ficino's

judged.justification: Sets differences from Ficino as the key to Pico's originality.

text: Howlett says Pico's God emerges as single but somehow twofold: a God of apophatic theology and an active creator from whom emanation or creation occurs who can be at least partially described.

quotes.text: Pico’s God emerges as single but somehow twofold: a God of apophatic or negative theology, and an active, creator from which emanation/creation occurs who can be at least partially described.

judged.justification: Offers a two-aspect God as the key to reading Pico on the One and Being.

text: Howlett says that in Pico's concordance Hokmah is also the Aristotelian active intellect and Christ, another potential end and the Ficinian home of being.

quotes.text: For in Pico’s concordance, Hokmah is also the Aristotelian active intellect and Christ (another potential end and the Ficinian home of ‘being’).

bears_on.note: Ficinian home of being placed in Hokmah/Christ

text: Howlett describes Ficino's first level as the angelic mind or intellectual, supracelestial world, combining the Christian sphere of the angels with the Plotinian intellect.

quotes.text: Ficino’s version is in the main Christian Plotinian but takes from other Platonic variants. We emanate from the One or God. The first level is the angelic mind or intellectual or supracelestial world, combining the Christian sphere of the angels with the Plotinian intellect.

bears_on.note: Ficino's angelic mind as second hypostasis

text: Howlett states that Pico uses the basic Ficinian structure while emphasizing Proclus and the sacred geometry of the universe (her own statement); she then quotes Pico's Heptaplus, which reports God presiding over nine orders of angels in the first world.

quotes.text: Pico uses this basic Ficinian structure while inevitably emphasizing Proclus more and consequently the sacred geometry of the universe.
In the first world, God, the primal unity, presides over nine orders of angels as if over as many spheres and, without moving, moves all toward himself.

bears_on.note: Pico's cosmology built on Ficino's structure

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Heptaplus that the three worlds are one world because whatever is in any of them is contained in each.

quotes.text: For ‘these three worlds are one world, not only because they are all related by one beginning and to the same end, or because regulated by appropriate numbers they are bound together both by a certain harmonious kinship of nature and by a regular series of ranks, but because whatever is in any of the worlds is at the same time contained in each

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Heptaplus that although the natures are mutually contained they are allotted separate seats and peculiar rights.

quotes.text: ‘Although the natures are mutually contained by each other, they are nevertheless allotted their separate seats and certain
peculiar rights.’11) just a highly complex and multilayered one.

text: Howlett says the Plotinian One is an atemporal unity while Pico's creator is located in a temporal framework, that the God of Kabbalism is the Ein-Sof, and that the Aristotelian First Cause is an unmoved mover involving action commensurate with a creator God.

quotes.text: But what else is this God? The Plotinian One is an atemporal unity, or singularity even, whereas Pico’s creator is specifically located in a temporal ... framework (however metaphorical). The God of Kabbalism is the Ein-Sof or nought. It does not act and cannot be known in any way. The Aristotelian First Cause is an unmoved mover (‘that which moves without being moved’)15 which at least involves action commensurate with a creator God.

text: Howlett argues that Pico's syncretic God is twofold and that Kabbalism allows this, positing both the Ein-Sof and the first sefira Keter, which partly shares the Ein-Sof's apophatic qualities yet begins the emanatory chain, so that the problem is knowing which he is referring to.

quotes.text: Pico’s syncretic God inevitably is twofold and Kabbalism allows for this structure, for it posits both the Ein-Sof and the first sefira, Keter or crown. Keter is the closest representation to the divine within the universe. It participates at least partially in the Ein-Sof’s apophatic qualities and is therefore partially hidden. But it is also the beginning of the emanatory/creative chain on the Tree of Life.
Pico’s God, One and First Cause is the Ein-Sof but is also Keter, as the partially revealed God. The problem is understanding which he is referring to and when.

open_questions.text: Which aspect of God (Ein-Sof or Keter) Pico refers to at a given point.

basis_quote.text: The problem is understanding which he is referring to and when.

judged.justification: A single interpretive key (Ein-Sof/Keter) for Pico's God-language.

text: Howlett says Pico's phrase the solitary darkness of the Father may sound like a description of the Ein-Sof but suggests rather the partially active principle of God as Keter.

quotes.text: So, Pico can talk about ‘the solitary darkness of the Father,’16 which may sound like a description of the Ein-Sof but suggests rather that he is referring to this partially active principle of God as Keter.

text: Howlett states that Pico's description of God in the Conclusions recalls the Ein-Sof and the God of Christian apophatic theology, and that Pico is taking us from Ficinian Platonism to the darkness of Pseudo-Dionysius.

quotes.text: Pico’s description of God in the Conclusions recalls above all the Ein-Sof

It is also the God of Christian apophatic theology, which means it is impossible to say what this God is, as opposed to what it is not. Pico is taking us from Ficinian Platonism to the darkness of Pseudo-Dionysius where blindness and understanding meet.18

warrants.text: Note 18 cites Riva (2012) for the Dionysian darkness.

bears_on.note: Pico moves beyond Ficinian Platonism toward Dionysian darkness

judged.justification: Places Pico's God-language beyond Ficino's Platonism toward Dionysius.

text: Howlett quotes Pico's De ente that in the ascent God is being itself, the one itself, the good itself, yet we are still in light, that God is above being, true, one and good, and dwells in darkness.

quotes.text: …God is being itself, the one itself, the good itself, and likewise truth itself. We have now advanced two steps, ascending to the darkness which God inhabits, purging from the divine names all blemish that is from the imperfection of the thing signified. There now remain two steps, of which one proves the deficiencies of names, the other reveals the infirmity of our intelligence. These names, being, true, one, good, mean something concrete, and, as it were, participated. Hence, we say that God is above being, above true,

above one, above good, since he is existence itself, truth itself, unity itself, goodness itself. But we are still in light. God, however, has established his dwelling in darkness. Therefore, we have not yet reached God.’19

bears_on.note: De ente's own statement that God is above being and one

judged.justification: Shows De ente itself ending in Dionysian ascent, complicating the reading of it as a plain equation of One and Being.

text: Howlett quotes Pico's De ente as placing God most eminently above unity, goodness, truth and existence, unintelligibly and ineffably above everything most perfect.

quotes.text: Until ‘…finally saying only this about God, that he is unintelligibly and ineffably above everything most perfect which we can either speak or conceive of him. Then we place God most eminently above even unity, goodness, truth, and existence, which we conceive.’20

text: Howlett distinguishes the God who is existence, truth and unity itself, still in light, from the unintelligible Pseudo-Dionysian God above even unity in darkness, and reads the former as comparable to the pleroma.

quotes.text: Above this is the unintelligible and ineffable Pseudo-Dionysian God who is ‘above even unity’ and lives in darkness. The former invites comparison with the Platonic gnostic pleroma, so full of attributes that it is ready to overflow and thereby emanate.

judged.justification: Reads De ente's two stages as pleroma and Dionysian darkness.

text: Howlett posits that the coordinated unity Pico names is Keter, a plenitude of attributes in one, while the abstract and uncommunicated unity is the Ein-Sof, and says Keter is God revealed in the universe.

quotes.text: For another potential way of understanding the difference is between what Pico calls the ‘abstract and uncommunicated unity’ of Ein-Sof and something he calls the ‘coordinated unity’ (a collection or plenitude of attributes in one) which I posit to be Keter.21 The Ein-Sof is the God of retraction. Keter is not, however, God per se. It is God revealed in the universe.22

hedge_words: which I posit to be Keter

warrants.text: Note 21 quotes Pico's Conclusion 11>4 for the two unities.

quote.text: Ein-Sof should not be counted with the other numerations, because it is the abstract and uncommunicated unity of those numerations, not the coordinated unity.

judged.justification: Howlett's own proposal for mapping the two unities.

text: Howlett says there is one God who can be talked about in two different ways, apophatically or, as a philosopher must before mystical ascent, by explaining what God is.

quotes.text: We are dealing with one God that can only be talked about or understood in two different ways, depending on whether we are using apophatic theology or trying to explain (as a philosopher such as Pico must before ascending to mystical experience) what God is

text: Howlett says it is hard to know which God Pico refers to, taking a Heptaplus passage on God as being itself and derived from nothing as an example.

quotes.text: So inevitably it is hard to know to which ‘God,’ Pico is referring. Another example from Heptaplus: ‘God alone, who is derived from nothing and from whom all things are derived, is a wholly simple and individual essence.
Finally, but importantly, this God is ‘being itself’ which we will consider further below.

text: Howlett notes that early Kabbalism was unsure whether Keter should be counted part of the Ein-Sof rather than a sefira.

quotes.text: Indeed, the relationship between the Ein-Sof and Keter is so strong that early Kabbalism was unsure whether Keter should be considered as part of the Ein-Sof rather than as a sefira.30

warrants.text: Note 30 cites Green (1997).

text: Howlett notes that prayer and ascent of a community of believers is also core to Pseudo-Dionysius, hence familiar to Pico, and that Pseudo-Dionysius borrows from Platonic gnostic traditions.

quotes.text: Judaism was not the only religion to relate a community of believers, prayer, and ascent. It is also core to Pseudo-Dionysius’ work and therefore familiar as a concept to Pico. Pseudo-Dionysius is also borrowing from Platonic gnostic traditions.

text: Howlett asks where the Plotinian One is, noting that Pico says God is being itself, potentially an Aristotelian argument, whereas Plotinus and Ficino consider the Plotinian One above being.

quotes.text: But where then is the Plotinian One? Is it Keter or the Ein-Sof? And what of the First Cause? Pico has told us that God is ‘being itself,’ potentially an Aristotelian argument, whereas the Plotinian One is considered, by Plotinus and Ficino, to be above being.

open_questions.text: Whether the One that Pico's De ente treats is Keter or the Ein-Sof.

basis_quote.text: Is it Keter or the Ein-Sof?

bears_on.note: Ficino's One above being versus Pico's being itself

judged.justification: Sharpens the exegetical question underlying the dispute.

text: Howlett says that in De ente Pico outlines an apparently Aristotelian view that being and the One are the same, equating the One with the First Cause, and argues this is also Plato's original perspective, later misinterpreted by his followers.

quotes.text: The question of ... being and God is the topic of Pico’s last finished work, Being and the One. There Pico outlines an apparently Aristotelian point of view that being and the One are the same, thereby equating the ‘One’ with the First Cause. But he argues that this is also Plato’s original perspective, later misinterpreted by his followers.

bears_on.note: the contested thesis

text: Howlett quotes De ente's report of the received Platonic view that the One is prior to being because the one is more simple and more universal, so that God, whose is the highest simplicity, is one but not being.

quotes.text: the one is more simple and more universal. For this reason they also say that God, whose is the highest simplicity, is one, but not that he is being.’34

text: Howlett states the problem as how the One can be more than one thing, and suggests, more persuasively as she puts it, that this may be another instance of the Ein-Sof/Keter separation: a Plotinian One above being as abstract unity, and a One containing being as creative principle.

quotes.text: The problem, simply stated, is how can the point of singularity, the unity, the undivided One, be more than one thing or is the One here (understood numerically) simply a misnomer for the ‘nought.’ More persuasively, this maybe another example of the Ein-Sof/Keter separation: there is a Plotinian One that is above being as ‘abstract’ unity or singularity, and a One that contains being and all other attributes of the divine as the creative, active principle (coordinated unity or pleroma) that necessarily must contain everything (as their cause) in order to overflow and become multiple.

judged.justification: Proposes a Kabbalistic key for reading De ente's One.

text: Howlett states that Plato's Parmenides and Sophist both state that being and the One are not the same, but Pico argues that nothing in the Parmenides is positively asserted and that it is nothing but a dialectical exercise.

quotes.text: Plato’s Parmenides and The Sophist both state that being and the One are not the same. But Pico argues that in Parmenides, for example ‘Nothing in the whole dialogue is positively asserted. If anything is asserted, still nothing is clearly found by which we may ascribe this sort of teaching to Plato.’ Further, Pico asserts ‘That book is certainly not to be included among his doctrinal works, since it is nothing but a dialectical exercise.

text: Howlett judges Pico's treatment of the Parmenides a weak parrying of an inconvenient text and says he sees it as a red herring followed by later Platonists but not Plato's own view.

quotes.text: In other words, Pico sees Parmenides as a ‘red herring’ followed by later Platonists, but not Plato’s point of view. This is a weak parrying of an inconvenient text, but part of a series of arguments that examine the relationship between being and the One from a variety of different perspectives.

judged.justification: A critical judgement on the Parmenides move.

text: Howlett says Pico's thesis is that Plato and Aristotle agree that the One contains being, making his One a plenitude rather than the solitary, hidden nought.

quotes.text: His thesis is that Plato and Aristotle agree that the One contains being, making his One here a plenitude rather than the solitary, hidden nought.

text: Howlett reports Pico's first argument in De ente that since nothing is outside all things but nothing itself, being includes all things, and the one cannot include more than being, nor fewer, so being and the one are equals.

quotes.text: since there is nothing outside all things except nothing itself, if being, understood in this way, excludes only nothing from itself, then without doubt being must include all things.
Nor does the one include fewer things than being, as they themselves admit. Therefore, being and the one are equals.’37

warrants.text: Note 36-37 cite De ente (1965c, 42-43).

text: Howlett says Pico's second argument apparently contradicts his first, reasoning that God is not being but is above being and is the one above being, which Howlett identifies as the Ein-Sof also as the Plotinian One.

quotes.text: His second argument apparently contradicts his first

For this reason, we may truly say that God is not being, but is above being, and that something is higher than being, that is, God, and since the title one is given to God, we may consequently say that he is the one above being.’38 This is the Ein-Sof also as the Plotinian One—a God above all things.

open_questions.text: Whether De ente's two arguments contradict or represent two aspects of God.

basis_quote.text: His second argument apparently contradicts his first

judged.justification: Finds a self-contradiction inside De ente resolved by the Ein-Sof/Keter reading.

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Conclusion that the grades of the universe can be divided in five ways, from that-above-being to truly-not-being, and places it in the group on Plato.

quotes.text: By the method of the extremes and the middle we can recognize that the grades of the universe can be appropriately divided like this in five ways: into that-above-being, truly-being, not-truly-being, not-truly-not-being, and truly-not-being.’ This is a conclusion from the group on Plato.

text: Howlett argues that the Ein-Sof/Keter division partially solves the inconsistency between a God above being (the atemporal Plotinian One) and a One that contains being, the coordinated unity allowing the One to contain the many.

quotes.text: There are inconsistencies here that are partially solved by the Ein-Sof/Keter division: first, between a God above being (who is the atemporal Plotinian One) and One (one) that contains being. Even in this reading, the One as Keter should not contain being per se, but obviously Pico is attempting to attach being to the divine in some way and the notion of a ‘coordinated unity’ allows for the One to contain the many.

judged.justification: Resolves the One/Being tension by a two-aspect God.

text: Howlett argues the distinction Pico consistently makes between formal being and causal being makes the riddle simpler: causal being, suggesting Aristotle's First Cause though he refers also to Plotinus, is the cause of the abstract concept being, as opposed to formal being.

quotes.text: Further, if we consider also the distinction he consistently makes between formal being and causal being in his work,40 then the riddle becomes even simpler. Causal being, suggesting Aristotle’s First Cause (though he refers also to Plotinus), is the cause of the abstract concept (being), as opposed to formal being, which is the abstract concept in and of itself.
Lohr (1988, 583) argues that Pico is attacking Ficino through Aquinas’ distinction between these different types of being.

warrants.text: Note 40 reports that Lohr (1988) argues Pico is attacking Ficino through this Thomist distinction between types of being.

quote.text: Lohr (1988, 583) argues that Pico is attacking Ficino through Aquinas’ distinction between these different types of being.

bears_on.note: Howlett reports Lohr's argument that Pico deploys the formal/causal being distinction (Aquinas's) specifically to attack Ficino.

judged.justification: Identifies the formal/causal being distinction as the mechanism of De ente's reconciliation.

text: Howlett reports Lohr's argument that Pico is attacking Ficino through Aquinas' distinction between different types of being.

quotes.text: Lohr (1988, 583) argues that Pico is attacking Ficino through Aquinas’ distinction between these different types of being.

bears_on.note: Aquinas's distinction as Pico's weapon against Ficino

judged.justification: Ties Aquinas directly to the Pico-Ficino quarrel over being.

text: Howlett says Pico argues in the Commentary that Platonists view God as the cause of everything, not a thing but the cause of all things and not intellect but the source of all intellect.

quotes.text: In the Commentary, Pico argues that Platonists view God as the cause of everything, ‘not a thing but the cause of all things, likewise that God is not intellect but is the source and principle of all intellect.’41

text: Howlett argues that the causal-formal-participatory distinction is at odds with Ficino's understanding of Platonism, quoting Pico's remark that these statements give great trouble to modern Platonists and that a distinguished Platonist was astonished at Plotinus saying God understands nothing.

quotes.text: This differentiation between the causal and the formal (and participatory, forming of course a triad) is at odds with Ficino’s understanding of Platonism: Pico says ‘These statements give great trouble to modern Platonists…. I remember that a distinguished Platonist once told me that he was much astonished at a statement by Plotinus, where he says that God understands nothing and knows nothing….

warrants.text: Note 43 cites Pico's Commentary (1986, 11-12) for the quotation.

bears_on.note: difference between Ficino's Platonism and Pico's causal reading of Plotinus

judged.justification: Locates a doctrinal, not merely tonal, gap between Pico and Ficino on the One.

text: Howlett says Pico's Platonism binds Aristotelianism and Platonism by rereading Aristotle through the lens of later Platonism, moving between kataphatic and apophatic theology.

quotes.text: We move necessarily between kataphatic and apophatic theology, and Aristotelianism and Platonism are bound together by a rereading of Aristotle through the lens of later Platonism.42

warrants.text: Note 42 cites Trinkaus (1995a).

text: Howlett argues that Pico's God as Ein-Sof is so far above us that only apophatic theology can apply, whereas the revealed divine within the void, carrying the kinetic energy of God, the emanated universe or Tree of Life, is part of kataphatic theology.

quotes.text: Pico’s God/One/First Cause as Ein-Sof is so far above us, and beyond, that only apophatic or negative theology can apply. But the revealed divine within the void carrying the kinetic energy of God—the divine lightning flash of the emanated universe, the Tree of Life—this is part of kataphatic or positive theology.

text: Howlett says Pico's universe is both emanated (Platonic) and created (Judaeo-Christian), and that the result is confusing.

quotes.text: So Pico’s universe is both emanated (Platonic) and created (Judaeo-Christian).50 But the result is confusing.

open_questions.text: How emanation and creation cohere in Pico's cosmos.

text: Howlett reports Craven's argument that in the Heptaplus the worlds are not emanated but direct acts of creation starting with the lower world.

quotes.text: Craven (1981, 109) argues, for example, that in Heptaplus the worlds are not emanated but are direct acts of creation starting with the lower world.

open_questions.text: Whether the Heptaplus worlds are emanated or created directly; Howlett's main text treats the universe as both.

text: Howlett lists Pico's quasi-dualisms: a hidden God and the One of plenitude; Ein-Sof and Keter; prime matter of privation and of potentiality; and an emanatory and a created universe.

quotes.text: Pico provides us with a series of quasi-dualisms: between a ‘hidden God’ and the One of plenitude; between the Ein-Sof and Keter; between the prime matter of privation and that of potentiality; and between an emanatory universe and a created one.

judged.justification: Summarises a structural pattern for reading Pico's God-language.

text: Howlett argues that with Aristotelian causality God as First Cause may only participate in the first hypostasis, and lays out a triad of causal being in the One, formal being in the angelic mind and participatory being in the rational soul.

quotes.text: For instance, we could argue that God, as First Cause, only participates in the first hypostasis, as its cause.53 In the Commentary, Pico portrays God as shining in the rational soul (the next level down) ‘by means of the Angelic nature in which it [the rational soul] participates.’54 In emanation God is present at every level. If we consider the triad of causal, formal, and participatory being with God as the First Cause, above and beyond the universe: there is causal being in the One, God has formal being in the angelic mind, which is why ‘being’ is present there, and then has participatory being in the rational soul or celestial world.

warrants.text: Note 53 cites Farmer (1998, 20) for the point about the first hypostasis.

judged.justification: Gives a three-place scheme of being that maps onto De ente's argument.

text: Howlett notes that both Ficino and Pico hold that all created beings desire beauty, but that in the Commentary Pico argues that God has no desire because he lacks nothing, so that the love of beauty is alien to Him.
