quotes.text: Ficino argues, and Pico agrees, that all created beings desire beauty.58 But in the Commentary, Pico argues that God does not have this desire: ‘It is enough for now to say that since God has no desire for anything outside Himself, being most perfect in everything and lacking nothing, this love of which we speak, the desire to possess the beauty of another, could not be more alien to Him.’

bears_on.note: agreement on desire of creatures for beauty; disagreement on God

text: Howlett says Pico's doctrine that beauty is a subcategory of the good differs from Ficino, who, as Pico argues, places beauty below the good in the first emanation.

quotes.text: In other words, for Pico, unlike Ficino, the beautiful is a subcategory of the good. God is both, but good here is primary and God is beauty because he is the good. Pico argues that Ficino’s Platonic God is both good and beauty equally, though Ficino places beauty below the good into the first emanation.61

warrants.text: Note 61 cites Howlett (2016, 72).

bears_on.note: Pico's disagreement with Ficino about beauty and the good

text: Howlett reports Pico's commentary saying that love is not in God as Marsilio believes, since that would be an imperfection, but is the love of creatures for Him, and cites Allen on how strange this is.

quotes.text: Therefore love is the cause of the production of everything which proceeds from God, understanding by love what Plato and our Poet understand, not love which might be in Him, as Marsilio believes, because then there would be imperfection in Him, but the love of his creatures for Him

Allen (2008, 91–92) points out how strange Pico’s point of view is here, for instance that the soul’s love for God is not reciprocated, that God does not love us, because this would be an imperfection.

bears_on.note: Pico's correction of Ficino on love in God

judged.justification: A doctrinal point of difference explicitly named against Ficino.

text: Howlett says that in his Platonism Pico disagrees with Ficino on love, beauty and the good, adopting alternative Platonic viewpoints based on Plotinus and Proclus, and that divine beauty must lie in the first world of the emanated universe, Ficino's angelic mind.

quotes.text: In his Platonism, he disagrees with Ficino in aspects of his definitions of love, beauty, and the good, but espouses alternative Platonic viewpoints particularly based on Plotinus and Proclus.73 This also means that God’s beauty and the endpoint of our love for the divine is not in the Ein-Sof and also not in Keter as the unity. We are looking and finding divine beauty elsewhere. It must be in the first world of the emanated universe, Ficino’s angelic mind.

bears_on.note: definitions of love, beauty and good

text: Howlett states that the first hypostasis is the supracelestial or intellectual world, called the angelic mind in Ficino's Christian Platonic universe, and that in Kabbalism it consists of the triad Keter, Hokmah and Binah, which is also for Pico the Trinity.

quotes.text: This first ‘hypostasis’ is the supracelestial or intellectual world, also known in Ficino’s Christian Platonic universe as the angelic mind. In Kabbalism, this world consists of a triad of sefirot: Keter, the crown or throne of God; Hokmah, the incomprehensible wisdom of God; and Binah or the understanding of God (where wisdom is given shape or form). This first triad is the chariot from the Merkavah tradition that carries God into the universe. It is also for Pico the Trinity: Father (alef or av)74; Son (bet), and Holy Ghost.

bears_on.note: Ficino's angelic mind as the Christian counterpart to the first triad

text: Howlett says the first triad of Keter, Hokmah and Binah is the Platonic Christian angelic mind, the realm of seraphim, cherubim and thrones, the top of Jacob's ladder, the place of the Metatron, the world of forms and of formal being.

quotes.text: This first triad of Keter, Hokmah, and Binah is also the Platonic Christian angelic mind and as such is the realm of the seraphim, cherubim, and thrones. It is the top of Jacob’s ladder and the level we try to reach from our starting point in Malkut. It is where the ‘higher’ shekinah resides (as opposed to the lower in Yesod or Malkut), and the place of the Metatron. It is the Platonic world of forms; and the world of formal being.

judged.justification: Maps the top angelic orders onto the first sefirotic triad.

text: Howlett states that Keter is the one plus nine, the primal unity presiding over the nine orders, and that Keter or Hokmah, most persuasively Hokmah, is Aristotle's Active Intellect.

quotes.text: This ‘primal unity’ is God the One as the active presence in the void: Keter or the enthroned divine, seated on a chariot, not the hidden God beyond. Keter is the one plus nine (which in sacred mathematics is the One plus nine orders of angels or the One and the three triads of the sefirot).
Keter or Hokmah, but most persuasively Hokmah, are Aristotle’s Active Intellect.

text: Howlett quotes Pico's conclusion that when Plato says Love was born from the union of Poverty and Plenty on the birthday of Venus, he means that the first love, the desire of beauty, was born in the angelic mind when the splendour of ideas began to shine.

quotes.text: When Plato says that Love was born from the union of Poverty and Plenty in the garden of Jove, on the birthday of Venus while the gods feasted, he means only this, that then the first love, that is, the desire of beauty, was born in the angelic mind when in it the splendor of ideas, though imperfectly, began to shine.’83

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Commentary that the Angelic Mind did not have its perfect natural being until Love was born and turned it to God, and that the ideas descend from God into the Angelic Mind, becoming imperfect through distance from God.

quotes.text: Indeed, Pico argues in the Commentary that ‘the Angelic Mind did not have its perfect natural being until Love was born, and he was the occasion of giving it that being
The Form which God gives to the Angelic Mind is nothing but the Ideas, which, as we said, are the first beauty. Therefore the Ideas descend into the Angelic Mind from God

text: Howlett quotes Pico that the Platonic forms are in their essence in the angelic mind, where they are first produced by God, and are in the rational soul by participation.

quotes.text: The Platonic forms or universals are ‘In their essence’ in the angelic mind, ‘in which they are first produced by God.’87 They are in the rational soul too but ‘by participation.’

text: Howlett argues that in Ficino's Christian Platonic universe the angelic mind is the home of being, whereas Pico distinguishes formal being in the angelic mind from the locations of causal and participatory being.

quotes.text: In Ficino’s Christian Platonic universe, the angelic mind is the home of being, whereas Pico distinguishes between formal being in the angelic mind, and the locations of causal and participatory being.

bears_on.note: Ficino places being in the angelic mind; Pico distinguishes causal, formal and participatory being

judged.justification: States the doctrinal point at which Pico's ontology departs from Ficino's.

text: Howlett says Pico reorganizes Ficino's hierarchy of forms or understands them differently, for instance making beauty a subspecies of the good.

quotes.text: But Pico reorganizes Ficino’s hierarchy of forms or understands them in a different way, for instance beauty becomes a subspecies of the good.

bears_on.note: reorganized hierarchy of forms

text: Howlett says that in Ficino's Christian Platonism the epistemological and ontological are linked, the world of forms combined with the mind of God, which can then also be Aristotle's agent or active intellect.

quotes.text: In Ficino’s Christian Platonism this link between the epistemological and ontological is maintained. The Platonic world of forms is combined with the mind of God (the intellectual world) which then can also be Aristotle’s agent or active intellect.

bears_on.note: Ficino's combination of forms, divine mind and active intellect

text: Howlett says Alexander of Aphrodisias argued that the active intellect was the agency of divine intelligence and was universal, and that Augustine connected the world of forms with the angelic sphere.

quotes.text: Alexander of Aphrodisias, one of Aristotle’s early commentators who also influenced Plotinus and late Platonism, argued that the active intellect was the agency of this divine intelligence and was universal, whereas the possible intellect belonged to each particular individual.
St Augustine formed a correspondence between Platonism and Christianity, connecting the world of forms with the angelic sphere.

text: Howlett says Averroes held both intellects universal and unified, Padua followed Averroes, and Aquinas disagreed, arguing that the active intellect is part of the individual mind.

quotes.text: Meanwhile, Averroes argued that both the active and the possible intellects are universal and unified98: leaving us with no particular intellect of our own. Padua primarily followed Averroes, Aquinas disagreed (see Summa Theologiae, I, q. 79, for example), arguing that the active intellect is a part of the individual mind.

text: Howlett argues that in Pico's universe the angelic mind is the world of forms with an active intellect, and that the Ein-Sof places much of the dynamism of the One into the angelic mind, perhaps supporting Ficino's attempt to bring act and dynamism from intellect to the One.

quotes.text: In Pico’s universe, the angelic mind is the world of forms, so there are universals. There is also an active intellect and it must be in the angelic mind too especially as Pico’s use of the Ein-Sof, places much of the dynamism of the One into the angelic mind (or in close proximity), relating intellect (whether as thought, wisdom, or understanding) to action, though not necessarily as the actor (perhaps supporting Ficino’s attempt to bring act and dynamism from intellect to the One).99

warrants.text: Note 99 cites Lohr (1988, 583).

bears_on.note: possible convergence with Ficino on act in the One

text: Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that ideas are the exemplary forms of natures and that things in the first level have causal being in the divinity and formal being in the angelic nature.

quotes.text: nothing but the exemplary Forms of the natures of things, and every intellect is full of them’ from the intellect of the angelic mind to the intellect of each individual soul.100 This is true of angels too: all things in the first level ‘have their causal being in the divinity as their original source and proceeding from Him immediately into the angelic nature have their second kind of being, formal.’101

text: Howlett says the angelic mind is home to angels with Christ present above them, that it can be called the son of God, and that in Kabbalism it is the home of the Metatron, the transfigured Enoch, who can prefigure Christ.

quotes.text: The angelic mind is home for a series of divine beings, including the angels. Christ is present above them.102 Indeed, the angelic mind can also be called the son of God, first because Christ is present, but secondly because it is what God causes: the most perfect effect that can be produced. In Kabbalism, it is the home of the Metatron, the transfigured Enoch,103 who can be a pre-figuring in the Old Testament of Christ.104

warrants.text: Note 104 cites Riva quoting Farmer for the Metatron symbols referring to the intellectual nature of the angelic mind.

quote.text: All these symbols, according to Farmer, would syncretically refer “to the intellectual nature of the angelic mind”

text: Howlett states that Abulafia's commentary on the Guide uses Maimonides to describe the Metatron as the agent intellect actualizing our intellect, an intellect detached from matter, the prince of the world and the angel of the Face.

quotes.text: The Metatron also serves at times in Kabbalistic literature as a synonym

for the active intellect, for instance Abulafia’s Commentary to the ‘Guide to the Perplexed,’ using Maimonides,105 describes the Metatron as the ‘thing that is actualizing our intellect from its potentiality’ which is ‘itself an intellect detached from any materiality.’ It is ‘the prince of the world… the angel of the [divine] Face… and its name is Sadday, like the name of its master and its cognomen is Metatron…and it is wise [and] speaking, the universal spirit, which has been called by the philosophers the Agent Intellect

warrants.text: Note 105 quotes Idel that Abulafia's exercise combines Ashkenazi esotericism with Neo-Aristotelian epistemology.

quote.text: Abulafia’s exercise is a combination of Ashkenazi esotericism, about an hypostatic son, who is the angel Metatron, with Neo-Aristotelian epistemology

judged.justification: Identifies the Metatron with the Agent Intellect through Abulafia and Idel.

text: Howlett argues that the Metatron can also be the ascended Enoch, the apotheosis of the seeker, implying that the mystic becomes a son by actualized intellect, a double intellectual sonship, and that the note finds this transformative understanding of intellectual activity also in Pico's Oration where the intellectual man can be an angel and son of God.

quotes.text: So, the Metatron can also be the ascended Enoch: thereby connecting God with the mystic, the seeker after God. The Metatron is the apotheosis of the seeker

There is then a ‘double intellectual sonship: that of the cosmic, who is the Agent Intellect, and an angel and son… and that of the mystic, who became a son by becoming an intellect in actu.’108 This suggests ‘a transformative understanding of the intellectual activity’ as in the Oration, where the intellectual man can be an angel and son of God.109

warrants.text: Notes 107-109 cite Idel (2014) for the double sonship and the Oration parallel.

judged.justification: Reads the Oration's intellectual angel-man through the Metatron/Agent Intellect tradition.

text: Howlett says that below the Metatron there are three ranks of three groups of angels making nine layers, thrones, cherubim and seraphim in the angelic mind, and principalities, archangels and angels in the celestial realm.

quotes.text: Below the Metatron (Christ or below Christ), there are three ranks of three groups of angels making nine different layers (again, nine plus one). Each of the three groups reflects a different level of the three worlds of the universe. In the angelic mind, the angels are the thrones, cherubims, and seraphim. For the second world, the celestial realm of planets, the angels are the principalities, archangels, and angels.

warrants.text: Note 111 cites Pico's Heptaplus (1965b, 110-11).

text: Howlett says angels are partly imperfect, at one remove from perfection, and quotes Pico's Heptaplus that the angel's double imperfection is that it is not being itself but an essence to which being comes by participation, and not intelligence itself but only happens to understand.

quotes.text: But angels are at least partly imperfect in that they are at one remove from perfection, and so adulterated by matter. Pico speaks of a ‘double imperfection’: ‘the one, that it is not being itself but only an essence to which being comes by participation, so that it may be; the other, that it is not intelligence itself but only happens to understand, since by its nature it is an intellect capable of understanding.’112

bears_on.note: angel as participated being, cf. De ente's being itself

judged.justification: Ties angelic imperfection to the distinction between being itself and participated being.

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Heptaplus that the angels understand God only so far as His nature is manifest in their own substance.

quotes.text: So ‘the angels understand God only so far as His nature is made manifest in their own substance….’113

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Heptaplus that true and perfect felicity carries us back to union with the beginning, that the angels can be raised to it but cannot ascend to it, and that man cannot go to that level but can be drawn.

quotes.text: The true and perfect felicity, however, carries us back to the contemplation of the face of God, which is the whole of the good, as He himself said, and leads us to perfect union with the beginning from which we sprang. The angels can be raised to this, but they cannot ascend to it…. To this level man cannot go, but can be drawn

text: Howlett says that in the Heptaplus Pico refers to Isaac, who relates the sefirot to the ten layers of the celestial world, the empyrean being the tenth sphere.

quotes.text: In Heptaplus, Pico refers to the Jewish philosopher, Isaac,120 who relates the sefirot to the ten layers of the celestial world. For instance, the empyrean is the ‘tenth sphere’ or ‘sapphire in the likeness of a throne, since the color of the sapphire signifies the splendor of its light, the likeness to a throne its immobility.’121

warrants.text: Note 120 identifies Isaac probably as Isaac ben Solomon Israeli.

text: Howlett says only nine realms of the celestial world are active, reflecting the nine-plus-one variant of the Tree and the nine levels of angels, and that the planets form triads in which Uranus is God, Saturn the first mind and Jupiter the world-soul, just as in Ficino.

quotes.text: But only nine realms are active within this world reflecting the nine plus One variant of the Tree of Life. This nine obviously uses again the Platonic and gnostic triads just as they reflect the nine levels of angels. The planets also form triads that reflect aspects of divine architecture: for instance, Uranus is God, Saturn is the first mind, and Jupiter is the world-soul, just as in Ficino.124

bears_on.note: planetary triad as in Ficino

text: Howlett states that in the Heptaplus and the Oration Pico describes the celestial world as needing the divine mover, in that heavenly bodies are adapted to circular motion but unable to perform it without being turned.

quotes.text: For ‘…the heavenly bodies, although adapted to circular motion, are not in themselves sufficient to perform this motion, but need the divine mover to turn and revolve them.

text: Howlett says that Pico's inconsistencies may be due to a change of views, problems of argument, an incomplete project or missed points, but more persuasively arise from attempting to combine what is partly similar and partly very different.

quotes.text: But similar viewpoints between texts argue for Pico’s consistency (direct disagreement is rare) and while his concordance was never completed, texts such as Heptaplus are supposed to be finished statements on aspects of that concordance. More persuasively, inconsistencies inevitably emerge when attempting to put together what is partially similar and what is partially very different.

judged.justification: Explains apparent contradictions as effects of concordism rather than change of mind.

text: Howlett poses the questions raised by Pico's metaphysics: how a hidden God can act, whether the One belongs to apophatic or kataphatic theology, whether the divine presence resides only in the angelic mind, and how emanation and creation co-exist.

quotes.text: How can a hidden God ever ‘act’? Is the One part of apophatic or kataphatic theology? Does the divine presence only reside in the angelic mind, or does it truly extend to all worlds? How can emanation and creation co-exist?

open_questions.text: Whether the divine presence resides only in the angelic mind or extends to all worlds.

basis_quote.text: Does the divine presence only reside in the angelic mind, or does it truly extend to all worlds?

text: Howlett reports that Pico told Barbaro he had turned from Aristotle to the Academy not as a deserter but as a scout, going to Ficino while suggesting that he was viewing Platonism as an Aristotelian, though Platonism became a key part of his outlook.

quotes.text: After a strong foundation in Aristotle, Pico tells Barbaro that he ‘turned recently from Aristotle to the Academy, but not as a deserter, as that author says, but as a scout’.25 He went to explore Platonism with the master at the center of the Platonic revival, Ficino, but suggests that he is simply viewing Platonism as an Aristotelian. This may have been true at the beginning, but Platonism became a key part of his philosophical outlook.

bears_on.note: Pico frames his study with Ficino as reconnaissance
letter to Barbaro

text: Howlett describes the relationship between Ficino and Pico as perplexing, inspiring and often antagonistic, Ficino portraying a deep friendship at least in retrospect and Pico seeing Ficino as his philosophical archnemesis.

quotes.text: The relationship between Ficino and Pico was perplexing, inspiring for both and often antagonistic in ways that are difficult to understand from their correspondence and work. Ficino, a relentless optimist, tends to portray a deep

friendship and love between the two, at least in retrospect, and Pico, the student who soon wishes to be the teacher, sees Ficino often as his philosophical archnemesis: the person to debate and prove wrong.

bears_on.note: antagonism and friendship in the relationship

judged.justification: States the asymmetry of self-presentation in the sources.

text: Howlett says Pico's first extended philosophical piece directly challenged Ficino's work on the Symposium, and that in doing so he became immersed in Plotinus, an author Ficino had only recently started to explore.

quotes.text: Pico’s first extended piece of philosophy was a commentary on Plato’s love theory, directly challenging Ficino’s own recent work on Plato’s Symposium. But in challenging Ficino, he becomes deeply immersed in Plotinus, choosing as the lynchpin of his Platonism an author Ficino had only recently started to explore.26

bears_on.note: first quarrel with Ficino over Plato's Symposium, via Plotinus

judged.justification: Links the origin of the dispute to Plotinus.

text: Howlett cites Pico telling Ficino that Plotinus had not left his thoughts and that he had Plotinus's works at hand and felt obliged to study him.

quotes.text: Pico tells Ficino: ‘This I know: Plotinus has not left my thoughts. Not only do I have his works at hand, but I feel obliged to study him as well. I have always admired him just as I do now’

warrants.text: Note 26 cites Bori (2012, 17 n24).

bears_on.note: Pico's stated commitment to Plotinus written to Ficino

text: Howlett states that in May Lorenzo sent word through Ficino that the returning Pico should live in Florence, lending him a villa at Querceto near Fiesole.

quotes.text: In May, Lorenzo sent word through Marsilio Ficino to the returning Pico that he should come and live in Florence, lending him a villa at Querceto near Fiesole.73

bears_on.note: Ficino as Lorenzo's messenger to Pico
villa at Querceto

text: Howlett reports a disputation at Lorenzo's house in 1489 between a Franciscan theologian and a Dominican, with Pico, Ficino and Lorenzo apparently siding with the Franciscan.

quotes.text: For instance, one well-sourced event was a disputation held at Lorenzo’s house in 1489 between a Franciscan theologian, Benigno Salviati, and the Dominican, De Mirabilibus with Pico, Ficino and Lorenzo apparently siding with the Franciscan.92

bears_on.note: Ficino and Pico on the same side at Lorenzo's disputation
host

text: Howlett says that, following Pico's threefold division of the soul, the highest part, intelligence, is shared with the angels, and that the intellect is illuminated by a greater, even divine, intellect which she glosses as the divine active intellect, the spirit of the lord or the Kabbalistic Metatron.

quotes.text: and above the intelligence which ‘we share no less with the angels….’60

The intellect is illuminated (in the Aristotelian sense) by a ‘greater, even divine, intellect… whether it be God (as some would have it) or a mind more nearly related to man’s…’ which we might call divine active intellect, the spirit of the lord or the Kabbalistic Metatron.62

judged.justification: Identifies the illuminating intellect as the Metatron.

text: Howlett says the intelligence is connected to the angelic mind of the universe, quoting Pico that intellects are eyes and that the power of the soul in which we are like the angels is called sight by all the Platonists.

quotes.text: The intelligence is connected to the angelic mind of the universe: ‘Intellects are eyes’ for ‘What the eye is among corporeal things, the mind is in the spiritual realm.’
The other is that power of the soul in which… it was said that we are like the angels. This power is called sight by all the Platonists, and corporeal vision is nothing but a copy of it.…

text: Howlett argues that Pico seems to suggest our intelligence is active, functioning in the Aristotelian manner, while also arguing that God's grace impels us, suggesting it is partly passive and needs a universal active intellect, and offers a third way in which the particular mind's upper level becomes an active intellect opened to the divine one.

quotes.text: Pico seems to suggest that our intelligence is active: we can see God and can choose to ascend toward the divine. If it is active, then it functions in the original Aristotelian manner. It abstracts from the particular to the universal, moving itself upward. However, he also argues that we are impelled to ascend through the motile power of God’s grace suggesting that our intelligence is at least partially passive
We could also argue a third way. The upper level of the particular mind could become (mobilized as) an active intellect

open_questions.text: Whether Pico's intellect is active, passive, or activated by the divine active intellect.

basis_quote.text: We could also argue a third way.

text: Howlett argues that if Pico's intellect is the Aristotelian active intellect it has a far stronger role than Ficino's, which tends to reflect the divine somewhat passively, and that epistemological concerns become more central in Pico as he amalgamates Aristotelianism with other traditions.

quotes.text: If the intellect is the Aristotelian active intellect, then Pico’s intellect, once activated, has a far stronger role than Ficino’s which tends to reflect somewhat passively the divine.
Epistemological concerns—what we can know, and how we can know it—become far more central in Pico’s philosophy in his effort to amalgamate Aristotelianism with other traditions.

hedge_words: If the intellect is the Aristotelian active intellect

bears_on.note: active versus reflective intellect

judged.justification: Puts an epistemological difference between Pico and Ficino.

text: Howlett says Ficino insists on the immortality of the soul, that Aristotle was ambiguous, and that Alexander of Aphrodisias, reading De anima III, held the active intellect to be outside the individual soul, while Averroes removed all that could be considered immortal in our souls.

quotes.text: Ficino insists on the immortality of the soul in Theologia platonica de immortalitate animorum, following Plato, who uses the argument of affinity in the Phaedo

Alexander of Aphrodisias refers to the third book of Aristotle’s De anima80 arguing that the active intellect is outside the individual soul, leaving the soul as mortal. Averroes removes all that could be considered immortal or incorruptible within our souls.

bears_on.note: Ficino's Platonic Theology on immortality

text: Howlett cites a note that Ficino's defence of the soul's immortality is a conscious reaction against later medieval thought, a fight in the name of Plato and Augustine against Aristotle or his commentators, and says Pico is left needing to bridge Averroism with immortality, an argument left unmade.

quotes.text: Ficino’s defense of the immortality of the soul, following the Byzantine philosopher, George Gemistus Pletho, is ‘a conscious reaction against later medieval thought, a reaction that would quite properly claim to be a fight in the name of Plato (and of Augustine) against Aristotle or, at least, against his commentators.’84 In his consistent attempt to try and bridge the Aristotelian and Platonic traditions, Pico is left potentially needing to bridge Averroism with the immortality of the soul, but this argument was left unmade.85

warrants.text: Note 84 cites Kristeller (1964a, 46); note 85 cites Farmer (1998, 20).

bears_on.note: Ficino's anti-Aristotelian stance on the soul

text: Howlett quotes Pico's commentary on which parts of the soul various ancient thinkers held immortal: Proclus and Porphyry the rational part only, Xenocrates and Speusippus also the sensitive, Numenius and Plotinus every soul.

quotes.text: Proclus and Porphyry will have it that only the rational part is immortal and all the others are corruptible. Xenocrates and Speusippus make the sensitive part immortal also. Numenius and Plotinus, adding even the vegetative part, conclude every soul to be immortal.’86

text: Howlett says Pico's Oration sends the ascending soul to the court of the cherubim, seraphim and thrones, the angelic mind, and quotes that the seraph burns with love, the cherub shines with intelligence, and the throne stands in judgement.

quotes.text: This is the court of the cherubim, seraphim and thrones, the sphere of the angels, the angelic mind, and reminiscent of Jewish palace literature. He tells us that ‘The seraph burns with the fire of love; the cherub shines with the splendor of intelligence; the throne stands in the steadfastness of judgement.’89

judged.justification: Identifies the Oration's three orders with the angelic mind.

text: Howlett states that henosis requires God's grace, the illumination of the Active Intellect activating our will, and that only we and the angels, of all created beings, can be drawn in this manner.

quotes.text: Henosis is achieved by God’s grace (the Aristotelian ‘illumination’ of the Active Intellect) activating our will in a final revelation of understanding in Binah which bonds us to the divine presence. Grace is required here for we ‘cannot go, but can be drawn.’93 Of all beings that have been created in God’s universe, we and the angels alone can be drawn in this manner.

text: Howlett says the God who is felicity is the Plotinian One but also the best of what can be thought of, meaning Keter rather than the Ein-Sof.

quotes.text: This is God as Plotinian One, but also as the ‘best’ of what can ‘be thought of’ meaning Keter, rather than beyond what can be thought or the Ein-Sof, or indeed the part of Keter that participates in the Ein-Sof.

text: Howlett states that the two ascents, through love and mystical ascent, come together in Kabbalism and Christian thought, especially Pseudo-Dionysius.

quotes.text: The two ascents come together in Kabbalism and Christian thought, especially that of Pseudo-Dionysius.

text: Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that love arouses a memory of the intellectual part and leads the purged soul to be most happily transmuted into angelic form.

quotes.text: where purged, as it were, by the fire of love, as we shall show in the following work, it is most happily transmuted into angelic form.’107

text: Howlett says the resting-place at the end of the ascent is not a unio mystica, in the sense of union with the One itself, and supports this by quoting Pico's commentary that the soul ends its journey at the sixth step, is not allowed to move on to the seventh, and rests at the side of the First Father.

quotes.text: The resting-place is not a unio mystica, in the sense of union with the One itself: ‘Reaching this, the sixth step in the sequence, the soul ends its journey, and it is not allowed to move on to the seventh, the sabbath, as it were, of heavenly love. Here it should rest happily in its goal, at the side of the First Father, the fountain of beauty.’115

text: Howlett states that Ficino's and Pico's ladders are not the same: Pico moves immediately away from earthly love, replaces Ficino's Platonic reminder of innate beauty with an Aristotelian abstraction while keeping a Platonic Idea at the end, and changes the poem so that we cannot ascend as far as God.

quotes.text: Ficino and Pico’s ladder are not the same. First Pico moves immediately from any suggestion of earthly love as a final or even temporary end.

Secondly, Pico changes Ficino’s (Platonic) approach that corporeal beauty reminds us of the embedded concept of real Beauty in our souls, for that more Aristotelian ‘abstraction’ while maintaining a Platonic Idea at the end of the ascent.123
Finally, and most importantly, Pico changes the poem so that we cannot achieve ascension as far as God.124

bears_on.note: two ladders

judged.justification: Lists three concrete differences between Ficino's and Pico's ladders.

text: Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that desire is sensitive, rational or intellectual, that is bestial, human or angelic, an intellectual and angelic will.

quotes.text: Every time that the thing desired is incorporeal and non-sensible the desire must be either an intellectual and angelic will or a rational choice raised and elevated to the sublimity of intellect.’ Love, as desire, can be ‘sensitive, rational, or intellectual,’ that is ‘bestial, human, or angelic.’

text: Howlett says Ficino argues that heavenly beauty descending into a human body imprints itself, somewhat equivalent to Pico's grace, though Pico says our souls form our bodies when we descend.

quotes.text: Ficino is more direct, arguing that heavenly beauty descending into a human body imprints itself on the body thereby making it beautiful: a direct reminder of heavenly beauty for the careful observer. Ficino’s imprint is somewhat equivalent to Pico’s ‘grace,’ though Pico does state that our souls ‘form’ our bodies when we descend into the world of nature,131 just that this is not a perfect process.

bears_on.note: Ficino's imprint doctrine compared with Pico's grace

text: Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that the soul which follows heavenly love is completely united with the Intellect and from a man becomes an angel.

quotes.text: The soul that follows heavenly love is ‘completely united with the Intellect and from a man he becomes an angel, wholly inflamed by this angelic love

text: Howlett quotes Pico's commentary that love makes men equal to angels, and says this was Enoch's fate, an intellectual rapture, transformed from man to angel.

quotes.text: This is the inestimable gift of love which makes men equal to angels, an admirable faculty which through death gives one life.’139 This is true for all of us if we pass fully to the intellect away from the corporeal and so we are ‘transformed from man to angel.’ This was Enoch’s fate: ‘an intellectual rapture’140

text: Howlett says that in the Heptaplus Christ opened a seventh or sabbatical exposition, and that our first aim is to become cherubim and our final apparent aim to be seraphim next to God.

quotes.text: To be clearer, Christ opened an extra interpretative approach to the texts handed down from Moses, called in Heptaplus the seventh or ‘sabbatical exposition.’ This interpretation returns us to God.

Our first aim is to become cherubim,144 allowing us to move up toward the Godhead, the sphere of love, and potentially down again to the life of action.145 Our final apparent aim is to be seraphim, next to God.

text: Howlett says Pico's henosis is similar to Ficino's with more emphasis on Plotinus, that in the body the soul reaches the edge of the celestial world and probably no further, and that Pico could be playing with triads, cherubim representing the celestial world and seraphim the angelic mind.

quotes.text: Pico’s approach to henosis is similar to Ficino’s, with more emphasis on Plotinus, 146 and in addition to Platonism, Kabbalism, more Christian mysticism and Aristotelianism.

But Pico could also be ‘playing’ with triads again: in the triad of cherubim, seraphim and thrones, cherubim could be representing the celestial world, as opposed to seraphim that represent the angelic mind).

open_questions.text: Whether cherubim represent the celestial world and seraphim the angelic mind in Pico's triad.

basis_quote.text: cherubim could be representing the celestial world, as opposed to seraphim that represent the angelic mind

bears_on.note: Pico's henosis compared with Ficino's

text: Howlett says Pico follows the threefold path of Pseudo-Dionysius from purification to contemplation to illumination.

quotes.text: But it also involves theology, and religious practice as Pico follows the threefold path of Pseudo-Dionysius: from purification, to contemplation, to illumination.

open_questions.text: Later (l. 8791) Howlett lists the Dionysian triplex via as cleansing, illumination, perfection; the two orderings differ.

basis_quote.text: cleansing, then illumination (through contemplation) and afterward perfection

text: Howlett says Ficino's focus is on return after a temporary sight of the angelic mind and renovatio, whereas Pico's focus is on the movement up.

quotes.text: Ficino’s focus is on return after temporary sight of the angelic mind. He portrays the journey as a ride on the chariot of the soul up through the heavens to the edge of the celestial sphere (the boundary with the angelic mind) where we can see the world of forms.
Pico may think of ascent as Jacob’s Ladder with angels going up and down, but his focus is on the movement up. Return or the practical outcomes of our experience are not his focus.

bears_on.note: difference of purpose: return versus ascent

judged.justification: Grounds the disagreement of purpose in the treatment of the ascent.

text: Howlett says Pico brings together philosophy, theology and religious experience as necessary for ascent, much as in Pseudo-Dionysius, Iamblichus and Proclus, and quotes Copenhaver that the Oration is a mystic's manifesto for ascent to self-annihilating union with God.

quotes.text: He emphasizes asceticism, poeticizes the mystical experience, and brings together philosophy, theology and religious experience (reason and faith) as necessary components of ascent, much as found in Pseudo-Dionysius, Iamblichus and Proclus. Indeed, Copenhaver asserts that the Oration is ‘a mystic’s manifesto for ascent, by way of magic and Kabbalah, to self-annihilating union with God.’152

warrants.text: Note 152 cites Copenhaver.

text: Howlett says Pseudo-Dionysius' three-stage path from the Celestial Hierarchy is purgatio, illuminatio and unitio or perfectio, and Iamblichus' curriculum is moral philosophy, dialectics, natural philosophy and theology, both matching steps in Pico's three pillars.

quotes.text: For example Pseudo-Dionysius’ three stage path (triplex via) from Celestial Hierarchy: cleansing, then illumination (through contemplation) and afterward perfection (purgatio, illuminatio, and unitio [or perfectio]).160 Or Iamblichus’ curriculum of moral philosophy, dialectics, natural philosophy and theology.161

judged.justification: Correlates Pico's three-stage ascent with Dionysian and Iamblichean sequences.

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Commentary that the descent of what is higher is not a real movement downward but its drawing us to itself, a compulsion to ascend, and concludes that this suggests no return once the soul has left the body for the angelic mind.

quotes.text: But angelic descent is complicated. In the Commentary, Pico tells us that we should not understand it as a genuine movement downward because what is higher cannot place itself lower, ‘but rather that by its own power it draws us to itself. Its descent into us is a compulsion upon us to ascend to it
First this concept of ‘descent’ suggests there is no return once the soul has left the body for residence in the angelic mind.

text: Howlett says that in the Oration Pico appears at times to agree that the divine presence couples with Binah, so that we do not ascend to the Active Intellect or Hokmah but are infused when we reach understanding, and that the mystic literally becomes the Agent Intellect, henosis as noesis.

quotes.text: In the Oration, Pico appears at times to agree, as the divine presence or shekinah couples with Binah. We do not ascend to the Active Intellect or Hokmah but are infused with the divine presence when we reach understanding (Binah).174

the mystic ‘literally becomes the Agent Intellect. The dissolution of his merely human self in the bottomless pool of the Godhead is the reward awaiting the mystic at the top of the ladder.’175 This is henosis as noesis.

judged.justification: Reads the Oration's ascent as noesis with the Agent Intellect.

text: Howlett reports Idel's argument that both Pico and Alemanno believe the soul can cleave to the Ein-Sof, and says she sees no evidence of this in Pico, whose language suggests the soul cleaves to Keter.

quotes.text: Indeed, Idel also argues that both Pico and Alemanno believe that the soul can ‘cleave’ to the Ein-Sof.176 I see no evidence of this in Pico. However confusingly interconnected Keter and the Ein-Sof may be, Pico’s language suggests that the soul ‘cleaves’ to Keter when he speaks of ascending to the First Father.

open_questions.text: Whether the soul cleaves to the Ein-Sof (Idel) or to Keter (Howlett).

basis_quote.text: I see no evidence of this in Pico.

judged.justification: Sets Howlett against Idel on the goal of the soul's ascent.

text: Howlett states that the obvious candidate for the Active Intellect among the sefirot is Hokmah, and that if the Active Intellect is our end point it is a form of noesis, with a more permanent noesis or even a form of henosis possible for those who die.

quotes.text: Which sefira is the Active Intellect is also clear. The obvious candidate is Hokmah as Divine Wisdom.

But if the Active Intellect is our end point, this is not unio mystica with the hidden God, nor even with its highest point in the universe, Keter. It is a form of noesis with even a temporary sight of the Active Intellect possible if we stay in the body.

text: Howlett states that Pico uses the Kabbalistic mors osculi or binsica for the ineffable union of the soul with God and its emancipation from materiality in the commentary and the Conclusions, and that in the commentary binsica, death from a kiss, is said to occur when the soul unites itself in intellectual rapture to things separate from it.

quotes.text: Pico uses the Kabbalistic trope of the ‘kiss of death’ (mors osculi, mittat neshikah in Hebrew, binsica in Pico’s Italian) for the moment of assimilation: the ‘ineffable union of the soul with God and its emancipation from materiality,’178 in both his Commentary and the Conclusions.

You will read nothing more in their books except that binsica, death from a kiss, occurs when the soul so unites itself in intellectual rapture to things separate from it that, uplifted from the body, it abandons it completely.’181

text: Howlett says Maimonides may have been Pico's source for the kiss of death in the Conclusions, though the Commentary adds Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, perhaps a triad of sefirot, and that the intellectual ecstasy of the kiss suggests noesis and not henosis.

quotes.text: Maimonides may have been Pico’s source in Conclusions, but in the Commentary he includes Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as founders of the tradition, which could simply represent a triad of sefirot.

This intellectual ecstasy echoes the Platonic furori, the inspirations or different types of madness found in Plato and Ficino, such as in Plato’s Symposium, the subject of Pico’s Commentary,183 it allows suggests noesis and not henosis.

bears_on.note: Platonic furori in Plato and Ficino

text: Howlett says that in the Commentary Pico agrees with Ficino on the kiss in which souls join, but that Pico's kiss is never given to another person and looks only to noesis or henosis without full union.

quotes.text: In the Commentary Pico agrees with Ficino that when two people kiss ‘Each transfers its own soul into the other with kisses; it is not so much that they exchange souls, as that they are so perfectly joined together that each of them can be called two souls, and both can be called a single soul.’184 But Pico’s kiss is never supposed to be given to another person.

bears_on.note: the kiss as shared doctrine, applied differently

text: Howlett argues that unlike Ficino, Pico does not discuss returning to the world with the blueprint from the glimpse of the divine, whereas in Ficino the returner is a divine magician able to change the world.

quotes.text: Unlike Ficino, Pico does not discuss returning to the world with the blueprint obtained from the glimpse of the divine, to change the world through the manipulation of the Tree.186

In Ficino, the returner is the ‘active’ ‘woke’ individual: a divine magician, able to change the world literally through knowledge of the relationship between the world of forms, the celestial sphere, and the natural world.

bears_on.note: return versus ascent, the disagreement of purpose

judged.justification: Restates the mission difference in terms of the returner.

text: Howlett says there is remarkable consistency between the commentary and Pico's methodology and views in De ente.

quotes.text: Obviously, views change, and arguments develop, but there is remarkable consistency between much of his earliest manuscript, the Commentary, and his methodology and views in On Being and the One.

judged.justification: Argues continuity between the Commentary and De ente.

text: Howlett says Pico's answer to the faith and reason divide differs greatly from Ficino's, who understands Christianity as coherent with Platonic philosophy and so makes Platonism central.

quotes.text: It differs greatly from Ficino’s, for example, who uses many of the same sources but who understands Christianity as coherent with Platonic philosophy (with a little encouragement), and thereby implicitly makes Platonism, a philosophy however mystical, central.

bears_on.note: difference in how faith and reason are reconciled

judged.justification: Summarises the Ficino/Pico difference as centrality of Platonism.

text: Howlett says that within Platonism Pico favors Plotinus and even more the baroque gnostic structures of Proclus, but owes most to Ficino.

quotes.text: Within Platonism, he particularly favors Plotinus, and even more, the baroque gnostic structures of Proclus, but owes most to Ficino.

bears_on.note: Pico's chief Platonic debt is to Ficino

text: Howlett says Kabbalism can be the hermeneutics for understanding Plato and Aristotle, and that Pico aims to show each tradition consistent with the other, even in strange cases such as his use of the Parmenides in De ente.

quotes.text: Kabbalism is therefore often at the center, and even can be the hermeneutics for understanding Plato and Aristotle.

He takes seriously his role as the prince of ‘concord’: aiming to show compatibility or basic agreement through his argumentation (not amalgamating, but showing how each tradition is consistent with the other), even in the strangest of cases (his use of Plato’s Parmenides, for example, in On Being and the One).

judged.justification: Frames concord as showing consistency, not amalgamation.

text: Howlett asks how to reconcile the hidden God of apophatic theology and Kabbalism with the unmoved mover and the Plotinian One, and finds it tempting to distinguish the Ein-Sof from the active presence of God in Keter.

quotes.text: How do we bring together the ‘hidden God’ of apophatic theology and Kabbalism with the ‘unmoved mover/First Cause’ and the Plotinian One?

It is tempting within the structure of Kabbalism to consider two versions of God: the Ein-Sof above and beyond in the darkness of unknowing, and the active, dynamic presence of God within our universe (the One of potentiality) as figured in Keter.

open_questions.text: How a hidden God, the unmoved mover and the Plotinian One are to be brought together.

basis_quote.text: How do we bring together the ‘hidden God’ of apophatic theology and Kabbalism

text: Howlett states as one of her re-evaluations that Pico's concord succeeds when it builds on similarities and shared histories but reveals significant difference, so that creation is complicated by emanation and the God of negative theology cannot be the pleroma.

quotes.text: Thirdly, his attempt at concordance between these three pillars is successful when it builds on similarities/shared histories but inevitably reveals significant difference, so that creation is complicated by the comparison with emanation and the God of negative theology cannot be the pleroma.

judged.justification: A programmatic statement of Howlett's thesis about limits of concord.

text: Howlett states that Pico's henosis is a cleaving not with a wholly transcendent One but with its active attributes within our universe, beginning with those of mind and understanding, and that it can be a noetic process in which our minds touch the Aristotelian active intellect.

quotes.text: This union is a ‘cleaving’ not with a wholly transcendent One, but with its active attribute/s within our universe, starting with those attributes associated with mind and understanding. In Pico, henosis can also be a noetic process, where our minds touch the mind of the Aristotelian active intellect.

judged.justification: Redefines the end of Pico's ascent as noetic contact with the Active Intellect.

text: Howlett describes Ficino as very much part of the collective desire for change and on a mission to renew the world, while Pico's journey was of the self, an ascetic personal journey of the soul with no second step of return and reform.

quotes.text: Ficino, is very much part of the collective desire for change. He was on a mission to renew the world

Pico is part of this desire for change too, but for him, this was a journey of the self: an ascetic, personal journey of the individual soul developing its relationship to God. He provided a blueprint for the journey upward, but with no second step of return and reform.

bears_on.note: mission of renovatio versus solitary ascent

text: Howlett quotes Pico's Oration in a note: with Dyonisio as interpreter, souls are first purged, then illuminated, and finally perfected.

quotes.text: Respondebit utique, Dyonisio interprete, purgari illos, tum illuminari, postremo perfici.

open_questions.text: Resolves the order queried elsewhere in this packet: the Oration's Dionysian sequence is purge, illuminate, perfect.

judged.justification: Fixes the order of the Dionysian triplex via cited by Pico.

text: Howlett cites Copenhaver that Pico's ascent has moral philosophy for purification, dialectics for clarification, natural philosophy for information, theology for meditation, and religious practice leading to divinization, described in the Oration as being apart in the Father's darkness, a phrase borrowed from Pseudo-Dionysius.

quotes.text: Copenhaver (2019, 360) describes Pico using moral philosophy for purification, ascending through to dialectics for clarification, natural philosophy for information and then onwards to theology for meditation
‘divinization’ described in the Oration as being ‘absolutely apart in the Father’s darkness’ to borrow from Pseudo-Dionysius.

text: Howlett reports Papio's suggestion that Pseudo-Dionysius has taken aspects of the Greek Eleusinian mysteries, linking the four frenzies to the three stages, and that three archangels represent the stages.

quotes.text: Papio suggests (Borghesi and Riva 2012, 90) that Pseudo-Dionysius has taken aspects of the Greek Eleusinian mysteries linking the four frenzies to the three stages, and the three Delphic precepts
Papio also points to three of the archangels to represent each stage (Raphael, Gabriel and Michael; God heals, God is strong and Who is like God?).

text: Howlett quotes Pico's conclusion that the Metatron of the Cabalists is without doubt what Orpheus called Pallas, Zoroaster the paternal mind, Hermes the son of God, Pythagoras wisdom and Parmenides the intelligible sphere.

quotes.text: That which among the Cabalists is called < Metatron > is without doubt that which is called Pallas by Orpheus, the paternal mind by Zoroaster, the son of God by Hermes, wisdom by Pythagoras, the intelligible sphere by Parmenides.’

warrants.text: Note cites Wirszubski (1989) for the Kabbalistic conclusions.

judged.justification: Shows Pico himself reading Parmenides' intelligible sphere as the Metatron, relevant to his De ente treatment of the dialogue.

text: Howlett cites Ogren for a note attributed to Ficino, from late 1479 or early 1480, stating that all Kabaliste hold the world created and souls created together at the start, and which dates the world by a Hebrew reckoning.

quotes.text: Ogren (2009b, 1 n1) citing Ficino (from late 1479/early 1480): ‘Omnes Kabaliste mundum creatum ponunt et motum cessaturum, sed animas ab initio simul create
‘Ficino’ uses uniquely Hebrew dating: ‘the world has lasted for 5240 years.’

bears_on.note: Ficino's own Kabbalistic notes before Pico's

judged.justification: Shows Ficino knew Kabbalistic doctrine before Pico.

text: Howlett cites Busi that a letter from Ficino to Domenico Benivieni concerns a debate in 1485 at Pico's house between Mondego, Flavius and a Jewish physician.

quotes.text: Busi (2006b, 175–76) cites a letter from Ficino to Domenico Benivieni regarding a debate in 1485 at Pico’s house between Mondego, Flavius and an ‘Avraham’ or Avraam, a Jewish physician

bears_on.note: Ficino writes about a debate in Pico's house
Flavius in the 1485 debate

text: Howlett cites Scholem that two traditions were combined to create the greater and lesser Metatron: the angel Yahoel, a lesser YHWH, and the Enochian tradition of Enoch as scribe.

quotes.text: Scholem (1987, 214) argues that two different traditions were combined to create this greater and lesser Metatron: the angel Yahoel, a lesser YHWH, and an Enochian tradition of Enoch becoming a scribe recording people’s actions.

text: Howlett cites a note that Garin, though treating Pico's occultism persuasively, sold Kabbalah short, preferring to foreground Pseudo-Dionysius and Hermeticism.

quotes.text: ‘Although Garin dealt with the larger compass of Pico’s occultism more persuasively than anyone before him, he sold Kabbalah short….’ (109–110) preferring to foreground Pseudo-Dionysius and Hermeticism (127).

warrants.text: Note attributes the view to Copenhaver (2019).

text: Howlett says Pico focused on Plotinus and several later Platonists but was always mindful of the positions of his former teacher Ficino, whom she calls his most important scholarly friend and rival.

quotes.text: Pico focused on Plotinus and several later Platonists but was always mindful of the positions of his former teacher, Marsilio Ficino.
including his intellectual point and counterpoint with Ficino, his most important scholarly friend and rival.

bears_on.note: Ficino as friend and rival
